review.summary: This paper proposes a new method to align an LLM with human preferences. Rather than using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on pairs of human-annotated instructions and responses, where the responses are guaranteed to be harmless, the authors use a three step process to generate harmful responses from the LLM and then have the LLM analyze its own response to see how it can improve. Then, during inference, a prompt is prepended with "harmless, ethical, and inoffensive" to encourage the LLM to give harmless responses. The authors show that this technique is better than SFT on the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset and is also better at defending against attacks from the Safety Dataset.

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a new method to align an LLM with human preferences. Rather than using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on pairs of human-annotated instructions and responses, where the responses are guaranteed to be harmless, the authors use a three step process to generate harmful responses from the LLM and then have the LLM analyze its own response to see how it can improve. The first step is to induce a harmful response from the LLM by adding words like "harmful, unethical, and offensive" in the prompt. The second step is to have the LLM analyze its harmful response to see what mistakes it made. The third step is to fine-tune the LLM on the instruction, harmful response, and the analysis. Then, during inference, a prompt is prepended with "harmless, ethical, and inoffensive" to encourage the LLM to give harmless responses. The authors show that this technique is better than SFT on the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset and is also better at defending against attacks from the Safety Dataset.

## Soundness
4

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
* The authors propose an interesting new technique for aligning LLMs that relies on the LLM to analyze its own responses. This is an important contribution to the field as it is hard to get humans to annotate lots of responses as harmful or not. 
* The authors show that their technique is better than RLHF and SFT at aligning an LLM on the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset. They also show that it is better at defending against attacks from the Safety Dataset.
* The authors also show that even a really simple SFT on just the harmful and harmless responses from the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset improves the helpfulness and harmlessness of the model.

## Weaknesses
* The authors do not compare against DPO (https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.06408) or RLAIF (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16943) which are SOTA techniques for aligning an LLM.
* The authors do not show how their technique compares to the SFT baseline where the responses are not guaranteed to be harmless.
* The authors do not show the alignment numbers for the model before any fine-tuning to see if their technique is actually improving over the pre-trained model.

For example, in Table 3, the first and second rows show that using mistake analysis can sometimes lead to an increase in harmfulness. review.summary: This paper proposes a set of methods for generating long-term, multi-person human motion sequences. The core idea is to build on a pretrained motion diffusion model, and use different methods to compose motions together. The first method, DoubleTake, generates long-term single-person motion sequences by generating a sequence of short motions that overlap in a “handshake” region. Another method, ComMDM, learns a small model that takes as input features from two separate motion diffusion models and outputs a correction to the activations of the models. This is used to generate two-person motion sequences. The final method, DiffusionBlending, generates motion sequences with control signals, such as root trajectory, in the style of classifier-free guidance. This is done by finetuning the original diffusion model to only keep the motion that needs to be controlled fixed, and allowing the other motion to be diffused normally. Then, multiple models can be blended together using the standard classifier-free guidance formula.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method requires additional finetuning of the original MDM model. I think this is okay, but I would appreciate a more detailed analysis of the tradeoff between the additional training time and the performance gains. It is not clear to me how much performance is gained by finetuning the models. Also, how does the quality of the finetuned model change as the amount of data is varied?
2. There is no discussion of the limitations or failure cases of the proposed methods. I would like to see a more thorough discussion of this. For example, the DiffusionBlending method seems like it would not work well for fine-grained control of many joints at once, as the experiments only show results for control of a single joint.
3. I would like to see a more detailed analysis of the second take. How much does it improve the results? What happens if there are more than two takes? Is there a limit on how much the second take can improve the results, or does it always improve the results?

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a set of methods for generating long-term, multi-person human motion sequences. The core idea is to build on a pretrained motion diffusion model, and use different methods to compose motions together. The first method, DoubleTake, generates long-term single-person motion sequences by generating a sequence of short motions that overlap in a “handshake” region. Another method, ComMDM, learns a small model that takes as input features from two separate motion diffusion models and outputs a correction to the activations of the models. This is used to generate two-person motion sequences. The final method, DiffusionBlending, generates motion sequences with control signals, such as root trajectory, in the style of classifier-free guidance. This is done by finetuning the original diffusion model to only keep the motion that needs to be controlled fixed, and allowing the other motion to be diffused normally. Then, multiple models can be blended together using the standard classifier-free guidance formula.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. The proposed methods are straightforward and sensible. The “handshake” idea for composing motion sequences is interesting and novel, and the idea of learning a small model to combine two MDMs is also clever.
2. The experiments are thorough and show the effectiveness of the proposed method. The proposed methods outperform baseline methods on the HumanML3D dataset.
3. The paper is well written, and the figures are well-designed.

## Weaknesses
1. The proposed method requires additional finetuning of the original MDM model. I think this is okay, but I would appreciate a more detailed analysis of the tradeoff between the additional training time and the performance gains. It is not clear to me how much performance is gained by finetuning the models. Also, how does the quality of the finetuned model change as the amount of data is varied?
2. There is no discussion of the limitations or failure cases of the proposed methods. I would like to see a more thorough discussion of this. For example, the DiffusionBlending method seems like it would not work well for fine-grained control of many joints at once, as the experiments only show results for control of a single joint.
3. I would like to see a more detailed analysis of the second take. How much does it improve the results? What happens if there are more than two takes? Is there a limit on how much the second take can improve the results, or does it always improve the results?

## Questions
1. Is there any reason why the HumanML3D metrics cannot be used for the two-person motion sequences?
2. The ComMDM model is learned from data with two fixed motion diffusion models. Is it necessary to have the same two models, or can the ComMDM model be used with different models? This would be useful for generating motion sequences with more than two people.

For two-person motion generation, the proposed method, ComMDM, learns a small network to predict the corrections for each person's motion from the intermediate activations of the diffusion model. For motion editing, the proposed method fine-tunes the pretrained model and uses DiffusionBlending to blend multiple models for composite control tasks. # Review

## Summary
This paper addresses the theoretical expressive capacity of Transformers. The paper proves that a Transformer with one self-attention layer, single-head, and softmax is a universal approximator for continuous permutation equivariant functions on a compact domain. This means that a Transformer with one self-attention layer can memorize the training dataset, which is an interesting result. The proof is constructive. The paper also provides experimental results with rank 1 self-attention to support the proof.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. This paper provides a new and interesting theoretical result on the expressive capacity of Transformers. It shows that one-layer Transformer is sufficient for memorizing the training set and approximating continuous permutation equivariant functions on a compact domain. This is a notable result. 

2. The paper also shows that hardmax attention is not a contextual mapping and that softmax attention is a contextual mapping. This provides a good contrast.

## Weaknesses
1. The paper is not well organized. The major part of the paper (page 6) is devoted to the proof of the main theorem. However, the proof is not very clear. There is no paragraph or equation numbering, making it hard to refer to specific parts of the proof. There are also no explanations of the notations used in the proof. Also, the proof is not well-written. It is hard to understand why each step follows. I think it will be better if the paper includes a sketch of the proof and the main paper highlights the major steps of the proof and the main conclusions. 

2. The paper provides experimental results with rank 1 self-attention. It would be better to also provide results with standard self-attention.

## Questions
1. The paper says that one-layer Transformer can memorize the training dataset. However, the proof is based on the assumption that the training data is well-separated. How do you ensure that the training data is well-separated in practice? 

2. The paper uses a rank 1 self-attention for the theoretical proof. Why is rank 1 self-attention used? Why not use full-rank self-attention? 

3. Is it possible to extend the proof to multi-layer Transformer? What are the difficulties?

review.summary: This paper studies the expressive power of the transformer model, and shows that the model with one self-attention layer is universal. The proof is constructive: it shows that there is a set of low-rank weight matrices that can implement a contextual mapping. This construction is based on the observation that softmax operator can separate vectors that are token-wise separated.

weaknesses.issue:
- The result is a bit incremental, as the main technique (softmax separates token-wise separated inputs) has already been used in the literature to show that transformer can be implemented by a two-layer model with sufficiently many hidden neurons. 
- The model that the paper shows to be universal is actually not the standard transformer model. The model is slightly different because the self-attention layer does not include the layer normalization, and the universal approximation theorem does not hold for any input sequence length $n$, but only for $n$ in a certain range (more on this in the questions). 
- The experiment does not fully support the main claim. If the hypothesis in the last paragraph of the paper is true, then the accuracy of the 1-layer model should eventually catch up with the larger models. It is thus reasonable to train the model for more epochs to see if the 1-layer model can indeed achieve the same performance as the 6-layer model.

# Review

## Summary
This paper studies the expressive power of the transformer model, and shows that the model with one self-attention layer is universal. The proof is constructive: it shows that there is a set of low-rank weight matrices that can implement a contextual mapping. This construction is based on the observation that softmax operator can separate vectors that are token-wise separated.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
- This paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- The proof is simple and clean. I especially appreciate the idea of using the separation power of the softmax operator.

## Weaknesses
- The result is a bit incremental, as the main technique (softmax separates token-wise separated inputs) has already been used in the literature to show that transformer can be implemented by a two-layer model with sufficiently many hidden neurons. 
- The model that the paper shows to be universal is actually not the standard transformer model. The model is slightly different because the self-attention layer does not include the layer normalization, and the universal approximation theorem does not hold for any input sequence length $n$, but only for $n$ in a certain range (more on this in the questions). 
- The experiment does not fully support the main claim. If the hypothesis in the last paragraph of the paper is true, then the accuracy of the 1-layer model should eventually catch up with the larger models. It is thus reasonable to train the model for more epochs to see if the 1-layer model can indeed achieve the same performance as the 6-layer model.

## Questions
- The assumption that the input sequences are token-wise separated is not sufficient for the universal approximation. The authors probably also need to assume that the input domain is bounded, so that the domain can be partitioned into finite number of $\epsilon$-nets, and each net is token-wise separated. This implies that the universal approximation theorem does not hold for any input length $n$, but only for $n$ in a certain range. In particular, it does not explain the success of the model on long documents. How do you think your result can be extended to handle this case?
- The model that the paper shows to be universal is actually not the standard transformer model, as it does not include layer normalization. Can your proof be extended to the standard model?
- It is not clear to me why the hardmax attention cannot separate token-wise separated inputs. The proof is a bit hard to follow, and I suspect the statement is actually false. Can you give a formal proof or a counterexample?

review.summary: The paper focuses on proving that a one-layer Transformer with softmax-based self-attention has a memorization capacity for finite samples. This is achieved by demonstrating that a single layer of self-attention with low-rank weight matrices can perfectly capture the context of an entire input sequence. The authors also show that Transformers consisting of one self-attention layer with two feed-forward neural networks are universal approximators for continuous permutation equivariant functions on a compact domain. The paper clarifies the connection between the softmax function and the Boltzmann operator, and proves that a single layer of self-attention with low-rank weight matrices possesses the capability to perfectly capture the context of an entire input sequence.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The paper is largely based on the work of [1] and [2], with the main difference being the reduction of the number of attention layers needed for memorization from $2n$ to $1$. However, the authors do not provide any insight into why the softmax function can achieve this reduction in layers.

2. The authors demonstrate that a single layer of self-attention with low-rank weight matrices can capture the context of an entire input sequence, but they do not provide a clear explanation of how the softmax function contributes to this capability.

3. The paper assumes that the input tokens are separated by a certain distance, which may not always hold in real-world scenarios. This assumption limits the generalizability of the results.

4. The paper focuses on the theoretical aspects of the Transformer model and does not provide any empirical validation of the proposed framework. Experimental results would strengthen the paper and demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed approach.


References:

[1] Kim, P., & Sontag, E. D. (2023). Provable benefits of self-attention in deep learning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 36, 29441-29457.

[2] Arechiga, N., & Yau, C. J. (2023). Transformers with softmax attention are universal approximators. arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.05198.

review.summary: The paper introduces a new task called Instruction-oriented Object Detection (IOD), which aims to enhance human-computer interaction by enabling object detectors to understand user instructions and locate relevant objects. The authors propose a model called Ins-DetCLIP, which leverages the knowledge within large-scale language models (LLMs) to empower the detector with instruction-following capabilities. The paper presents a dataset called IOD-Bench, which consists of instruction-guided detections and specialized evaluation metrics. The authors should consider highlighting the specific novel aspects of their approach and how it differs from existing methods.

2. The paper does not provide a comprehensive comparison with existing methods, such as open-vocabulary object detection methods or instruction-following models. It would be beneficial to compare the proposed Ins-DetCLIP model with these existing approaches to demonstrate its advantages and limitations.

3. The paper could provide more details about the implementation of the Ins-DetCLIP model, such as the specific architectures used for the visual encoder and the LLM, the training procedure, and the hyperparameters. This would enhance the reproducibility of the proposed approach.

review.summary: This work introduces a new task called Instruction-oriented Object Detection (IOD), which enables object detectors to comprehend user instructions and identify relevant objects. To address this task, the authors have developed a dataset called IOD-Bench and a model named Ins-DetCLIP. The proposed Ins-DetCLIP model leverages the extensive knowledge within large language models (LLMs) to enable the detector to follow instructions. It employs a visual encoder to extract object-level features, which are then aligned with the input instructions using a cross-modal fusion module integrated into a pre-trained LLM. The experimental results on IOD-Bench demonstrate that Ins-DetCLIP outperforms baseline methods that directly combine LLMs with detection models.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The motivation for the proposed IOD task is not strong enough. In the introduction, the authors present a scenario where a domestic robot should be able to recognize targets like "beverages," "drinks," and "cups" when instructed to "hand me a cup of drink." However, it is worth noting that the proposed IOD task still requires the explicit naming of target categories such as "beverages," "drinks," and "cups," which contradicts the initial motivation of eliminating the need for a list of target categories. Additionally, in real-world scenarios, it is more natural to provide a list of target categories rather than a complex instruction. For example, when a user wants to find a cup on a desk, it is more straightforward to simply say "find me a cup" rather than "find me something on the desk that I can drink from." Therefore, it would be beneficial for the authors to further discuss the advantages of the proposed IOD task over traditional open-vocabulary object detection.
2. The technical contribution is limited. The proposed Ins-DetCLIP model is quite similar to InstructBLIP, as both models utilize a vision encoder to extract object-level features and align them with text instructions using a cross-modal fusion module. The main difference is that Ins-DetCLIP focuses on predicting the category name of objects, while InstructBLIP focuses on extracting different visual features. However, the idea of predicting the category name of objects has already been explored in previous work, such as DetCLIPv2.
3. The comparison with existing methods is not comprehensive. In the experiments, the authors compare Ins-DetCLIP with baseline methods that directly combine LLMs with detection models. However, there are other related works that should be considered for comparison, such as InstructBLIP and DetCLIPv2. Additionally, it would be beneficial to compare the performance of Ins-DetCLIP with traditional open-vocabulary object detection methods on the IOD-Bench benchmark.

However, it is worth noting that the proposed IOD task still requires the explicit naming of target categories such as "beverages," "drinks," and "cups," which contradicts the initial motivation of eliminating the need for a list of target categories. Additionally, in real-world scenarios, it is more natural to provide a list of target categories rather than a complex instruction. For example, when a user wants to find a cup on a desk, it is more straightforward to simply say "find me a cup" rather than "find me something on the desk that I can drink from." Therefore, it would be beneficial for the authors to further discuss the advantages of the proposed IOD task over traditional open-vocabulary object detection.
2. The technical contribution is limited. The proposed Ins-DetCLIP model is quite similar to InstructBLIP, as both models utilize a vision encoder to extract object-level features and align them with text instructions using a cross-modal fusion module. The main difference is that Ins-DetCLIP focuses on predicting the category name of objects, while InstructBLIP focuses on extracting different visual features. However, the idea of predicting the category name of objects has already been explored in previous work, such as DetCLIPv2.
3. The comparison with existing methods is not comprehensive. In the experiments, the authors compare Ins-DetCLIP with baseline methods that directly combine LLMs with detection models. However, there are other related works that should be considered for comparison, such as InstructBLIP and DetCLIPv2. Additionally, it would be beneficial to compare the performance of Ins-DetCLIP with traditional open-vocabulary object detection methods on the IOD-Bench benchmark.

- The authors should provide more results on ImageNet-based pre-training and downstream tasks. MAE has demonstrated strong performance on ImageNet classification and KITTI object detection. - The authors claim that the proposed method can be used for interactive segmentation. However, there are no experiments to support this claim.

- In the experiments, the authors only compare the proposed method with MAE. However, there are many other self-supervised representation learning methods, such as BYOL and SimCLR. The authors should also compare the proposed method with these methods.

This is motivated by the fact that learning from regions may help the model to be less biased towards raw pixels and focus more on the grouping of pixels that encode parts, objects, and scenes.
Specifically, the paper proposes `masked Region Autoencoding’ (RAE) to learn from regions. RAE can be combined with MAE in a straight forward manner.
Experiments on COCO show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The main concern is that the paper only shows results on COCO, which is not enough. As MAE has shown, results on ImageNet is important to evaluate the visual representation learned by the model. I think the main reason is that the model has been trained on COCO, so it is not surprising that it can perform well on COCO downstream tasks. But it is not clear whether it can work well on other datasets, for example ImageNet. 

2. The paper claims that learning from regions can help the model to be less biased towards raw pixels and focus more on the grouping of pixels that encode parts, objects, and scenes. But there are no experiments to support this claim. In my opinion, this claim should be easy to verify by training the model on ImageNet, and then do linear evaluation on ImageNet. If the model is more focused on the grouping of pixels, it should perform worse on ImageNet linear evaluation. 

3. In Table 1e, it seems that RAE$\rightarrow$MAE performs better than RAE$\leftarrow$MAE. Is there any explanation for this?

This is motivated by the fact that learning from regions may help the model to be less biased towards raw pixels and focus more on the grouping of pixels that encode parts, objects, and scenes.

2. Experiments on COCO show the effectiveness of the proposed method over MAE.

## Weaknesses

I think the main reason is that the model has been trained on COCO, so it is not surprising that it can perform well on COCO downstream tasks. But it is not clear whether it can work well on other datasets, for example ImageNet. 

2. The paper claims that learning from regions can help the model to be less biased towards raw pixels and focus more on the grouping of pixels that encode parts, objects, and scenes. weaknesses.issue:

The paper proposes a region-aware pretraining method for vision transformer. 3

3. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

1. The performance of the proposed method is not comparable with MAE on ImageNet classification. It indicates that the learned representation may be not good for global recognition. It may be better to have a discussion on this phenomenon.

In MAE, the model is trained to reconstruct the image from the mask. The task is kind of self-supervised because the mask is obtained from the image. In the proposed method, the model is trained to reconstruct the region from the mask. The task is still self-supervised because the mask is obtained from the image. review.summary: The paper proposes to extend Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to also predict the segmentation mask (or region proposal) of an image. This is motivated by the fact that words are discrete in nature and it may be beneficial to have discrete tokens for images as well. This is achieved by learning a joint model that regresses both the original image and the regions. In order to avoid the high cost of processing each region independently, the paper proposes to use the query mechanism from DETR to efficiently process all regions in a single forward pass. The method is shown to work well with off-the-shelf region proposal algorithms such as Felzenswalb-Huttenlocher (FH) and Segment Anything Model (SAM). The model is pre-trained on COCO and evaluated on COCO, LVIS, and ADE20K datasets. It outperforms MAE on COCO and LVIS object detection and instance segmentation. It also obtains competitive performance on ADE20K semantic segmentation.

weaknesses.issue:
- The idea of predicting regions instead of pixels is not well-motivated. The paper does not provide enough evidence for why this is beneficial. The paper should have discussed this in more depth. For example, is there a way to visualize what information is encoded in the regions? Does the model obtain any semantic meaning from the regions? This is evidenced by the interactive segmentation results, but this is not the focus of this work.

- The results on semantic segmentation are weak. The method obtains significantly worse results than the current state-of-the-art. The paper should have discussed this and provided some explanations. I do not think this is a deal-breaker, but this should have been addressed.

- The paper only experiments with ViT backbones. It would be nice to see how the method works with other architectures such as Swin and ConvNeXt.

## Summary
The paper proposes to extend Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to also predict the segmentation mask (or region proposal) of an image. This is motivated by the fact that words are discrete in nature and it may be beneficial to have discrete tokens for images as well. This is achieved by learning a joint model that regresses both the original image and the regions. In order to avoid the high cost of processing each region independently, the paper proposes to use the query mechanism from DETR to efficiently process all regions in a single forward pass. The method is shown to work well with off-the-shelf region proposal algorithms such as Felzenswalb-Huttenlocher (FH) and Segment Anything Model (SAM). The model is pre-trained on COCO and evaluated on COCO, LVIS, and ADE20K datasets. It outperforms MAE on COCO and LVIS object detection and instance segmentation. It also obtains competitive performance on ADE20K semantic segmentation.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The idea to extend MAE to predict discrete regions is interesting and novel to the best of my knowledge.
- The results on COCO and LVIS object detection and instance segmentation are strong. The method outperforms MAE by a significant margin.
- The qualitative results are also impressive. The model seems to learn to attend to the object regions when prompted with a query box.

## Weaknesses
- The idea of predicting regions instead of pixels is not well-motivated. The paper does not provide enough evidence for why this is beneficial. The paper should have discussed this in more depth. For example, is there a way to visualize what information is encoded in the regions? Does the model obtain any semantic meaning from the regions? This is evidenced by the interactive segmentation results, but this is not the focus of this work.

review.summary: The paper introduces a novel pre-training method that extends the masked autoencoder (MAE) with region priors. The authors propose learning a region-based autoencoder that predicts binary masks in addition to the standard pixel-based autoencoder that is trained in parallel. The region-based autoencoder takes a set of region proposals (FH, SAM or ground truth) as input and predicts the corresponding binary mask. The decoder produces a set of masks that are encouraged to match the input mask, but are also able to reconstruct the pixel map, so there is a cross-pixel information flow between the two autoencoders. The method is shown to be effective in improving the performance of MAE when trained on COCO, both for the COCO and ImageNet datasets.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The method is only evaluated with MAE. It would be interesting to see if it works with other methods like BeiT or iBOT.
2. The method is only evaluated with ViT. It would be interesting to see if it works with other architectures like Swin or ConvNeXt.
3. The paper does not provide a clear answer on why the method works. There is a clear performance gap between MAE and R-MAE when trained on COCO, but not on Imagenet. How come?

review.summary: This paper presents a method for predicting factual errors in language models by analyzing the attention patterns of the model. The authors define factual queries as constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), where a factual error occurs when a constraint is not satisfied. They find that the magnitude of the attention contribution from constraint tokens to the last token correlates with the popularity of the entity and the correctness of the LLM. Based on this observation, they propose a method that predicts factual errors by probing the attention weights. The method is evaluated on 10 datasets with over 40,000 prompts and achieves comparable performance to the LLM's confidence in predicting factual errors. The authors also demonstrate the potential of their method to enable early stopping and fine-grained feedback.

weaknesses.issue:
- The method requires access to the internal attention weights of the LLM, which may not be feasible for black-box models.
- The performance of the method is highly dependent on the quality and complexity of the dataset. For example, it is unclear how to compute the popularity of the entity in some datasets. In other datasets, it may be unclear how to isolate the constraint tokens.
- The method is limited to conjunctions of constraints and may not be applicable to other types of queries.
- The performance of the method is similar to the model’s confidence, and adding confidence to the set of features seems to improve the results. In this case, it is unclear what is the real contribution of the attention-based method.

## Summary
This paper presents a method for predicting factual errors in language models by analyzing the attention patterns of the model. The authors define factual queries as constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), where a factual error occurs when a constraint is not satisfied. They find that the magnitude of the attention contribution from constraint tokens to the last token correlates with the popularity of the entity and the correctness of the LLM. Based on this observation, they propose a method that predicts factual errors by probing the attention weights. The method is evaluated on 10 datasets with over 40,000 prompts and achieves comparable performance to the LLM's confidence in predicting factual errors. The authors also demonstrate the potential of their method to enable early stopping and fine-grained feedback.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The paper provides a new perspective on understanding the factuality of LLMs by framing it as a constraint satisfaction problem.
- The authors conduct extensive experiments and analyses to validate their findings and proposed method.
- The method has practical applications in identifying factual errors early in the inference process, potentially leading to cost savings.

## Weaknesses
- The method requires access to the internal attention weights of the LLM, which may not be feasible for black-box models.
- The performance of the method is highly dependent on the quality and complexity of the dataset. For example, it is unclear how to compute the popularity of the entity in some datasets. In other datasets, it may be unclear how to isolate the constraint tokens.
- The method is limited to conjunctions of constraints and may not be applicable to other types of queries.

The key innovation is a hierarchical mesh structure that enables long-range interactions and fast collision propagation. The HCMT consists of two Transformers: a Contact Mesh Transformer (CMT) for contact dynamics and a Hierarchical Mesh Transformer (HMT) for long-range interactions. The method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and shows improved performance over existing approaches.

3

2. The HCMT demonstrates superior performance over existing methods on multiple benchmark datasets, indicating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
3. The paper provides a new dataset, the Impact Plate dataset, which is a valuable contribution for evaluating contact mesh simulation methods, especially in the context of manufacturing applications.

## Weaknesses
1. The paper could benefit from a more thorough comparison with existing methods, particularly in terms of runtime performance and scalability. While the HCMT is shown to outperform other approaches in terms of accuracy, it is not clear how it compares in terms of computational efficiency.
2. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the sensitivity of the model to its hyperparameters, such as the number of levels in the hierarchical structure.
3. The paper could provide more insight into the limitations of the proposed method and potential areas for future work.

review.summary: This paper proposes a graph transformer for simulating the dynamic interactions between deformable objects. The main claimed contribution is the usage of two types of edges: mesh edges and contact edges. The former represents the connectivity of each object, while the latter represents the connection between objects in contact. The proposed method adopts a multi-level graph structure and processes the finer graph first. This design enables the model to capture long-range dependencies. The proposed method is evaluated on three datasets, including two plates and a sphere. The proposed method is compared against two baselines: MGN and GT. The proposed method achieves a superior performance.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The authors claim that the proposed method can better model long-range dependencies. However, there is no evidence to support this claim. I think the multi-level design is the main reason for this, rather than the design of the contact edge. Moreover, multi-level design has already been explored in previous works, such as EAGLE [1] and MSMGN [2].
2. The experimental results are not convincing enough. The baselines are old and not state-of-the-art. I suggest the authors to compare with recent baselines such as EAGLE [1] and EagleSim [3]. Moreover, the authors only conduct experiments on simple geometries such as plates and a sphere. It would be great to see the performance on more complex geometries such as the HOOD dataset used in [3].
3. The model does not take time as an input. This means the model has to be trained for different time intervals. This is not a desired property for a simulator.
4. The number of levels is fixed during training and cannot be adjusted during inference for runtime optimization.

review.summary:
The paper proposes a method to improve the reasoning performance of LLM by self-checking.
The self-checking is implemented by checking each reasoning step of the LLM-generated response and regenerated by the LLM and comparing the two.
The authors conduct experiments on three math datasets, showing some improvements over the baseline.

weaknesses.issue:
1. Although the idea of using LLM to self-check its reasoning is interesting, the proposed method seems not very reliable and practical. 
- The proposed method relies on the LLM to perform many subtasks, such as target extraction, information collection, step regeneration, and result comparison. However, it is not clear how to ensure the reliability of these subtasks. For example, if the information extraction is not accurate, the following subtasks will be affected. 
- The performance of the proposed method highly relies on the LLM. For example, the information extraction stage will rely on the capability of the LLM to extract the target, and the accuracy may vary a lot for different LLMs.
- The proposed method is only evaluated on three math datasets. How to extend it to other tasks and domains is unclear. 
- The proposed method requires many LLM calls to finish the reasoning process, which is not practical in real-world applications.

2. The experiment results are not very promising. 
- The proposed method only shows marginal improvements on two datasets. On the math dataset, the performance gain is only 1%~2% over the simple baseline, majority voting. The improvement is even negative on the GSM8K dataset. 
- The authors did not compare with the state-of-the-art performance on these datasets, making it hard to judge the effectiveness of the proposed method. 
- It is unclear how many LLM calls are required to implement the proposed method. The author should include such an analysis in the paper.

review.summary:
The paper proposes a method for LLMs to check their own multi-step reasoning. 
The method is a zero-shot method that uses the LLM to individually check the conditional correctness of each step in a chain of reasoning.
The key to the method's success is a multi-stage approach to check each step that uses the LLM's generative strengths and decorrelates errors between the original generation and checking. 
The method is evaluated on three math tasks and shows improved performance compared to simple majority voting and other baselines. 
The method provides an estimation of confidence for each solution, which can be used to filter out solutions with low confidence. 
The paper includes ablation studies to justify key design choices and a discussion of the limitations.

weaknesses.issue:
The paper does not explain how to handle cases where the LLM is wrong at the step of target extraction, information collection, or step regeneration. These steps are essential for the method's success, and if the LLM makes errors at these steps, it can propagate those errors to the final answer. The paper should address how to handle such cases or discuss their impact on the method's performance.

The paper only evaluates the method on three math tasks. It would be beneficial to evaluate the method on other domains and tasks, such as logical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and symbolic reasoning, to demonstrate its generalizability and versatility. The paper should include a discussion of the potential limitations and challenges of applying the method to other domains.

The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the computational cost and efficiency of the method. The paper should report the number of API calls required for each experiment and compare the computational cost of the method to the baselines. This would help readers understand the practical trade-offs of using the method.

The paper does not provide a comparison of the method with a simple baseline that generates multiple solutions and filters out solutions with low probability. The paper should include this comparison to show the advantages of using the method over this baseline.

review.summary: The authors propose to improve stability of backpropagation through time by zeroing out (in the backward pass) the derivatives w.r.t. to the input of the neural network. This is motivated by the fact that the time evolution of the simulation (the "physics") is typically stable, and the instability of BPTT is assumed to come from the interaction between the network and the simulator. Empirical evidence is provided for the effectiveness of this method on three problems.

weaknesses.issue:
My main concern is that the proposed method is not as novel as it seems. In the context of reinforcement learning, it is well-known that the derivatives of the reward with respect to the state (i.e., the "physics") is the critical component causing the instability of BPTT (when unrolling for more than one step). This is known as the "deadly triad" (see [1]). The solution to this problem is to truncate BPTT to 1 step. It seems like the authors propose a variant of this method specifically for supervised learning, but the principle is the same: truncate the derivatives through the network, keep the derivatives through the simulator.

[1] "The Deadly Triad of RL, BPTT, and HF-GAEs", Diuk, Cohen, Littman, 2018

review.summary: This paper considers the problem of balancing gradients in BPTT by zeroing out components that would cause the gradient to blow up or vanish, in particular in physics simulation settings.

weaknesses.issue:
* This paper only addresses the problem of vanishing/exploding gradients in a very simple setting where the simulator is a map S: (x, u) -> x' (whereas in general, it is a map S: (x, u, p) -> (x', p')), and the only input to the policy is the state (and not the history of states).  However, in this setting, it is known that the gradient can be backpropagated through time without exploding, using the "zero-init" trick (zero-initializing the policy before unrolling, and then learning the policy starting from the initial state, see e.g. https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.11728).  The authors do not cite this paper, and do not compare against this simple baseline, which is standard practice.

* The authors should consider more complex environments (e.g. the DeepMind Control Suite) and more complex policies (e.g. recurrent neural networks) in order to be able to make a convincing case that their method is effective.

* The authors should consider the related work on optimization for reinforcement learning, which also frequently considers the problem of vanishing/exploding gradients, and often considers the case where the simulator is a map S: (x, u, p) -> (x', p') (e.g. see https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13349, https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02453).

review.summary: The paper proposes a modification to the backpropagation through time algorithm for training neural networks to control dynamical systems. The motivation is that the gradient flow through the neural network can cause the magnitude of the updates to grow or shrink over time, leading to either explosions or vanishing of the gradients. This effect is particularly pronounced when unrolling the trajectory for a long time. To alleviate these issues, the authors propose to "stop" the gradients from flowing back through the neural network, and only backpropagate through the dynamics function, which the authors assume is "well-behaved". The backpropagated gradients are then modified to ensure that they are not entirely orthogonal to the gradients from the regular BPTT, to ensure that the neural network still learns something.

weaknesses.issue:
- The main assumption of the paper is that the gradient flow of the dynamics function $S(x, c)$ is well behaved, and thus can be used as a good "anchor" for the backpropagated gradients. This however assumes that the dynamics function is well-behaved, which is often not the case for contact-rich physics systems, which are often of the most interest. For these systems, the gradient flow can have discontinuities, and thus be highly anisotropic, which would violate the assumption of the proposed method.
- The experimental evaluation is lacking in terms of comparisons with relevant baselines. In particular, there is a large literature on learning to control dynamical systems with neural networks, including methods like TD learning, actor-critic methods, and hybrid methods that combine neural networks with classical control methods. These methods do not suffer from the same problems as BPTT, and should be used as a baseline. In addition, since the authors only use simple toy examples, it is unclear how well the proposed method would scale to more complex problems.
- The paper states that the gradients from the modified BPTT are "balanced", but this is only true in the toy example. In general, the gradients can still explode or vanish depending on the dynamics function, the neural network, and the loss function. The claim that the gradients are balanced needs to be more carefully qualified.

The key idea is to modify the gradients from back-propagation through time by zeroing out the partial derivatives of the controller with respect to its input. This is because the partial derivatives of the controller with respect to its input is not well-behaved in many cases, and could be zeroed out while still allowing gradients to flow through the simulator. weaknesses.issue:

review.summary: The authors propose to replace the backpropagation through time (BPTT) gradient with a modified version which they argue is better suited for training neural networks for simulators. The authors argue that the vanilla BPTT gradient has two main shortcomings: (1) the gradient magnitude explodes/vanishes along the optimization trajectory, and (2) the gradient has a rotational component that complicates convergence. The proposed method addresses (1) by only backpropagating through the simulator, and addresses (2) by zeroing out gradient components that are opposite in sign to the standard BPTT gradient. The authors demonstrate their method on a variety of control tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
1. While I found the toy examples to be helpful in illustrating the issues with gradient flow, I am not convinced that these issues are significant in more complex tasks. In particular, the authors claim that the rotation in the gradient field leads to slow convergence to minima. However, I would argue that this is actually a good thing in many cases, as it allows the network to explore different regions of the parameter space in its search for a global minimum. In fact, methods such as SAM [1] actively encourage non-zero curl in the gradient field to achieve this effect. In the context of neural simulators, I believe that a recent work by Battaglia et al. [2] is particularly relevant. In this work, the authors show that simply stopping gradient flow in certain components of the loss can lead to significant performance gains in neural network-based physics simulations. I would be interested to see a discussion of this work in the related work section, and how the proposed method compares to the approach taken in [2].


2. My main concern with the proposed method is that it appears to be quite similar to the method proposed in [2]. Both approaches essentially stop gradient flow in certain components of the loss, with the proposed method stopping gradient flow in the network output while [2] stops gradient flow in the simulation state. While the proposed method appears to achieve better performance in the tasks studied in the paper, I would argue that the method in [2] is more general in that it can be applied to any simulation. On the other hand, the proposed method can only be applied to simulations that involve a distinct separation between the simulation state and the network output. I would be interested to see some discussion of this point, and to see the proposed method compared to the method in [2] on one of the tasks studied in the present paper.


[1] Foret, P., Kleiner, A., Mobahi, H., & Neyshabur, B. (2021). Sharp minima can generalize for deep nets. ICML.

[2] Battaglia, P., Novello, H., Pasqualini, R., & Franco, L. (2021). Stop gradient and keep simulating: A simple strategy to stabilize training of neural simulators. NeurIPS.

The paper introduces \nola{}, a novel method for compressing LoRA models by leveraging linear combinations of random basis matrices. The authors address the limitations of existing low-rank adaptation techniques, such as the parameter count being lower-bounded by the rank of decomposition and dependence on the model architecture. \nola{} reparameterizes the low-rank matrices in LoRA using linear combinations of randomly generated matrices and optimizes the linear mixture coefficients, decoupling the number of trainable parameters from both the rank and network architecture. This method allows for higher compression ratios compared to LoRA and achieves comparable performance in terms of accuracy.

## Strengths
* The paper addresses significant limitations in existing LoRA models, such as the rank-one lower bound and dependency on model architecture, which are crucial challenges in model compression and adaptation.

# Review

## Summary
This paper presents a new method to improve upon Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). LoRA is a technique used to fine-tune large language models (LLMs) by training low-rank matrices that can be added to the original model weights. The proposed method, named nola, re-parameterizes these low-rank matrices as linear combinations of random basis matrices, allowing for a more compact representation. This decouples the number of trainable parameters from the rank and model architecture, enabling higher compression ratios. NOLA also incorporates quantization of the coefficient vectors for further storage reduction. The authors evaluate nola on both language and vision tasks using models like GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and ViT. Results show that nola achieves comparable performance to LoRA with significantly fewer parameters, especially for large models like LLaMA-2 70B, where it is 20 times more compact without sacrificing accuracy.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
- The paper introduces a novel reparameterization technique for LoRA, allowing for higher compression ratios by decoupling the number of parameters from the rank and model architecture.
- NOLA demonstrates significant parameter reduction compared to LoRA, especially for large models like LLaMA-2 70B, achieving a 20x compression without loss in accuracy.
- The approach is evaluated on both language and vision tasks, showcasing its versatility across different domains and model architectures.
- NOLA can be further enhanced with quantization of the coefficient vectors, providing additional storage savings.
- The method is applicable to various architectures beyond transformers, making it a promising technique for compressing large models in general.

## Weaknesses
- The paper does not provide a clear explanation of the motivation behind using a linear combination of random basis matrices for reparameterization. It would be beneficial to elaborate on why this specific approach was chosen and how it contributes to the overall performance and compression.
- The paper claims that nola can be further improved by quantizing the coefficients. However, the current version of the manuscript lacks a detailed discussion on the implementation and performance of this quantization process. Providing more information on how quantization is implemented and its impact on model performance would enhance the clarity and completeness of the paper.
- While the paper compares nola to LoRA, it does not provide a comprehensive comparison to other state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques. Including a broader range of baselines would help to better position nola in the context of existing literature and highlight its unique advantages.
- The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the training time and memory footprint of nola compared to LoRA. While it mentions that nola has a small overhead during training, a more in-depth comparison of the computational and memory requirements would provide a better understanding of the practical implications of adopting nola.
- The paper does not provide a thorough discussion of the limitations of the proposed method. It would be valuable to address potential challenges or scenarios where nola may not perform as well as LoRA or other baselines.

## Questions
- Could you provide a more detailed explanation of the motivation behind using a linear combination of random basis matrices for reparameterization? How does this approach contribute to the overall performance and compression of the model?

- Could you provide a more detailed analysis of the training time and memory footprint of nola compared to LoRA and other baselines? How does nola's computational and memory requirements compare, and what are the practical implications of adopting this method?

This model extends the capabilities of the commonly used Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron model in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs). The LM-H model addresses the limitations of the LIF model by dynamically regulating membrane-related factors and effectively balancing the extraction of historical and current information. The paper proposes the Learnable Multi-hierarchical (LM-H) neuron model for SNNs to address the limitations of the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model, such as gradient calculation failures in deep residual networks and inability to effectively utilize historical information. The LM-H model has wider calculation scope and can extract global information along the time dimension and propagate gradients in deep networks. The paper also develops a progressive STBP training algorithm to optimize the membrane-related parameters of LM-H neurons and proposes an efficient training framework to enhance the energy efficiency of SNN learning. Experimental results show that the LM-H model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets and network architectures.

## Soundness
4

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
4

## Strengths
The paper proposes a novel neuron model, the Learnable Multi-hierarchical (LM-H) model, that addresses the limitations of the widely used Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model in SNNs. The LM-H model has wider calculation scope and can extract global information along the time dimension and propagate gradients in deep networks. The paper also develops a progressive Spatio-Temporal Back-Propagation (STBP) training algorithm to optimize the membrane-related parameters of LM-H neurons. The algorithm can dynamically regulate the extraction ratio between historical and current information, leading to improved network performance. The paper proposes an efficient training framework that includes hybrid training and time-slicing online training to reduce the computational overhead and enhance the energy efficiency of SNN learning. The framework can significantly save energy consumption and memory costs compared to traditional STBP methods. The paper conducts extensive experiments on various datasets and network architectures to validate the effectiveness of the LM-H model and the progressive STBP training algorithm. The experimental results show that the LM-H model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets and network architectures, outperforming previous methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. The paper also discovers a "Long-Range Performance Reward" phenomenon, where the model's precision can be further improved as the number of time-step increases during the inference stage. This indicates that the learned membrane-related parameters can effectively extract information over a prolonged time range.

## Weaknesses
The paper does not provide a clear explanation for the choice of the specific form of the scalable-shiftable sigmoid learning function used to optimize the membrane-related parameters of LM-H neurons. It would be beneficial to provide more details on the design rationale and the advantages of this function over other possible functions.

The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the impact of the different values of the scaling factors ($\mu_D^l$, $\mu_S^l$, $\lambda_D^l$, $\lambda_S^l$) on the model performance and stability. It would be valuable to investigate how these factors affect the learning dynamics and the final accuracy of the model.

The paper lacks a comprehensive evaluation of the computational complexity and memory requirements of the proposed LM-H model and training framework, compared to other existing methods. It would be helpful to provide a detailed analysis of the computational cost and memory footprint of the proposed approach, especially for large-scale applications.

The paper does not provide a thorough discussion of the biological plausibility and interpretability of the LM-H neuron model. While the model is shown to be effective in improving SNN performance, it would be valuable to explore the biological inspiration and constraints of the model and its components.

## Questions
See above.

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a method to compute the gradient of a quadratic program (QP) with respect to parameters of the QP, which is a common need in machine learning. The proposed method leverages a notion of conservative Jacobian (which is essentially an approximate Jacobian) to resolve the infeasibility of the QP. Numerical results on the sudoku problem are presented.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
The problem is relevant, timely and well-motivated, since there is a lot of interest in using optimization as layers in neural networks, and the QP is one of the most important optimization problems.

The proposed method appears to be novel, and it is a nice idea. Moreover, the method is general (applies to any QP) and can be implemented without domain knowledge (unlike some previous methods).

## Weaknesses
The main issue with this paper is that the presentation is too terse, and many questions remain unanswered. I elaborate on this in the questions below. In summary, the paper could use some work in terms of writing and presentation to reach its full potential.

## Questions
The paper mentions that the augmented Lagrangian method is used to compute the ECJ. In what sense is the solution to the augmented Lagrangian method an approximation of the ECJ? It would be good to quantify the approximation (e.g. in terms of the duality gap).

In Section 4.1.2 the paper mentions that "by incorporating a potential optimal shift $s^*$ in its formulation" in order to handle the infeasibility of $Ax=1$. How exactly is this done? Is $s^*$ computed by solving a QP subproblem at each iteration? How does this affect the size of the QP?

What is the size of the QP in the numerical results? For how many variables and constraints?

How is the QP used in the numerical results formulated? What is $H$, $g$, $A$ and $u$?

Why is $Ax=1$ infeasible in the numerical results? Is it because $A$ is random and $x$ is drawn randomly?

The paper states that the augmented Lagrangian is used to compute the ECJ. What is the cost of computing the ECJ? How does this affect the overall computational cost of backpropagation? How does this compare with the baselines OptNet and CvxpyLayer?

The paper mentions that the augmented Lagrangian solves for $s$ (which corresponds to the $\ell_2$-distance to feasibility). How does the choice of $s$ affect the accuracy of the ECJ? What is the effect of using an inaccurate $s$?

The paper mentions that the augmented Lagrangian solves for $s$ by solving a QP. What if the QP subproblem is inaccurate? How does the accuracy of the subproblem solver affect the accuracy of the ECJ?

The paper mentions that the augmented Lagrangian solves for $s$ via a primal-dual method. What is the advantage of using a primal-dual method over a primal or dual method?

review.summary: The paper proposes a new method to learn the parameters of infeasible QP layers. The key idea is to extend the definition of the solution to QP to also include the closest feasible QP. This is done in a way that can be used in an optimization layer by relying on the notion of conservative Jacobian. The paper shows that this new definition of solution covers the solution of traditional differentiable QP when it is feasible and the least-square solution when it is not. The paper proposes practical ways to compute the Jacobian in both forward and backward passes. The paper shows that this new approach enables the training of a wider variety of QP layers. The new method is validated by an experiment on the classic Sudoku puzzle.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The paper's contribution is limited to QPs, while other types of quadratic layers, such as those with non-convex constraints, are not addressed.
2. The paper does not provide a detailed comparison with other methods for learning infeasible QP layers, such as the one proposed by Dontchev and Rockafellar (2009).
3. The paper does not provide a proof that the proposed method is consistent with the traditional Jacobian when the QP is feasible.
4. The experiment on the Sudoku puzzle is limited to a single problem and does not provide a comparison with other methods.

## Summary
The paper proposes a new method to learn the parameters of infeasible QP layers. The key idea is to extend the definition of the solution to QP to also include the closest feasible QP. This is done in a way that can be used in an optimization layer by relying on the notion of conservative Jacobian. The paper shows that this new definition of solution covers the solution of traditional differentiable QP when it is feasible and the least-square solution when it is not. The paper proposes practical ways to compute the Jacobian in both forward and backward passes. The paper shows that this new approach enables the training of a wider variety of QP layers. The new method is validated by an experiment on the classic Sudoku puzzle.

## Soundness

## Presentation

## Contribution

## Strengths

2. The paper is well written and easy to follow.

review.summary: This work proposes a method to differentiate through infeasible quadratic programs (QPs) using augmented Lagrangian techniques. This enables the training of QP layers that may be infeasible during training but are feasible at test time. This is shown to improve performance on the sudoku problem.

weaknesses.issue:
- While the method is well-motivated, the application domain seems quite narrow. It is only demonstrated on the sudoku problem, which is a special kind of linear program (LP) that is also a QP. However, the authors claim that their method is for differentiable QPs in general. It would be helpful to see experiments on more general QP problems with more general constraints, such as $Ax \le u$, $x^T H x \le 0$, etc., that are not LPs. This is especially important because these types of problems are more general and commonly studied in the QP literature. It would also help to see if the proposed method is actually useful in these more general cases.

- The proposed method does not seem to have much to do with machine learning. It would be helpful to see if the method is useful for any machine learning task other than sudoku. The authors claim that their method enables more structured learning with better predicting power, but this has not been demonstrated outside of sudoku. It would be helpful to see if the method can also improve performance on other machine learning tasks such as those in the Cvxpylayers benchmark, such as least squares and image classification.

- The proposed method seems to have limited novelty. It seems like the proposed method is a straightforward application of augmented Lagrangian methods for differentiating through QPs. However, it would be helpful if the authors could clarify any non-trivial aspects of this application.

review.summary: The paper proposes a method for the differentiation of (possibly infeasible) quadratic programs with linear constraints with respect to some parameters of the QP. Specifically, the authors propose to extend the definition of the solution of the QP to include also infeasible QPs by considering the solution of the closest feasible QP as the solution of the QP, where the distance is measured in the $\ell_2$ sense. Using the augmented Lagrangian method the authors then compute the corresponding conservative Jacobian of the solution map of the QP with respect to the parameters. The authors illustrate the proposed method with the example of the Sudoku puzzle, where the QP is a mixed integer linear program (MILP), however, the QP layer in the network does not need to compute a solution to the MILP but only to a relaxed LP.

weaknesses.issue: The main weakness of the paper is the lack of motivation and impact of the proposed method. The only example provided is the Sudoku problem, which is a MILP with linear constraints and integer variables. In this case, the QP layer in the network does not need to compute a solution to the MILP but only to a relaxed LP. Hence, the QP layer could be replaced by a linear layer without any (practical) difference. Indeed, the authors report in Section 4.1.1 that the QP layer learns to a solution of the LP relaxation and then uses the optimal basis of the LP as the $A$ matrix in the MILP (without the integer constraints). Hence, the proposed method seems to be a detour to solve an LP. The authors mention that one of the benefits of their method is that it is more robust than existing methods, however, this is not shown in the paper. The only results reported are the training and test errors of the different methods. Since the MILP can be solved by standard methods (such as Gurobi) in reasonable time, one could also train a QP layer by solving the MILP with Gurobi in each iteration and compare this baseline to the proposed method. This would show whether the proposed method has any benefits in terms of accuracy, run-time etc.

# Review

## Summary
The paper proposes a method for the differentiation of (possibly infeasible) quadratic programs with linear constraints with respect to some parameters of the QP. Specifically, the authors propose to extend the definition of the solution of the QP to include also infeasible QPs by considering the solution of the closest feasible QP as the solution of the QP, where the distance is measured in the $\ell_2$ sense. Using the augmented Lagrangian method the authors then compute the corresponding conservative Jacobian of the solution map of the QP with respect to the parameters. The authors illustrate the proposed method with the example of the Sudoku puzzle, where the QP is a mixed integer linear program (MILP), however, the QP layer in the network does not need to compute a solution to the MILP but only to a relaxed LP.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The paper is well written and the proposed method is sound. The authors present the proposed method in an accessible way and provide a good overview over related work. In contrast to previous work, the proposed method is able to deal with infeasible QPs and can hence be applied to a larger class of problems.

## Weaknesses
The main weakness of the paper is the lack of motivation and impact of the proposed method. The only example provided is the Sudoku problem, which is a MILP with linear constraints and integer variables. In this case, the QP layer in the network does not need to compute a solution to the MILP but only to a relaxed LP. Hence, the QP layer could be replaced by a linear layer without any (practical) difference. Indeed, the authors report in Section 4.1.1 that the QP layer learns to a solution of the LP relaxation and then uses the optimal basis of the LP as the $A$ matrix in the MILP (without the integer constraints). Hence, the proposed method seems to be a detour to solve an LP. The authors mention that one of the benefits of their method is that it is more robust than existing methods, however, this is not shown in the paper. The only results reported are the training and test errors of the different methods. Since the MILP can be solved by standard methods (such as Gurobi) in reasonable time, one could also train a QP layer by solving the MILP with Gurobi in each iteration and compare this baseline to the proposed method. This would show whether the proposed method has any benefits in terms of accuracy, run-time etc.

## Questions
- What is the motivation for using the augmented Lagrangian method to compute the Jacobian? Can this be replaced by any other method (e.g. using automatic differentiation)?
- What is the impact of the proposed method? Are there any problems, where the proposed method is really needed?

review.summary: This paper presents LILO, a neuro-symbolic framework for library learning. LILO consists of three components: (1) a synthesis module that uses both LLM-guided search and enumerative search to generate programs, (2) a compression module that uses stitch to identify abstractions, and (3) an auto-documentation module that uses an LLM to generate human-readable names and docstrings. weaknesses.issue:
- The authors do not evaluate LILO on DreamCoder's original benchmark, which is more comprehensive and widely-used. The authors argue that the original benchmark requires more than two CPU-months to run DreamCoder, and instead evaluate a subset of problems on three domains. However, I believe that the evaluation should be done on the full benchmark, with the runtime of DreamCoder distributed across multiple CPU-hours. I also believe that the authors should include DreamCoder's original results in the paper for reference. Furthermore, while the authors claim that DreamCoder takes two months to run, DreamCoder's wall-clock runtime is only 3.5 hours in total, so it is not prohibitively expensive. I am not convinced by the authors' claim that they improve on DreamCoder's performance by 20x in runtime.
- The LLM used in this work is Codex, which is a relatively weak model compared to GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, StarCoder, etc. It is hard to judge how well the proposed method would perform with stronger models.
- The authors do not discuss the cost of LILO in terms of LLM API costs and/or number of tokens.
- The authors do not compare against baselines from the literature, such as LAPS.
- The authors do not compare against baselines that use LLMs for program synthesis without library learning.
- The authors do not discuss how AutoDoc affects the LLM's ability to generate programs.
- The authors do not discuss how the choice of search algorithm (beyond the ablation) affects performance. For example, is A* more effective than breadth-first search?
- The authors do not discuss the impact of varying the size of the seed set.

The paper overemphasizes the neurosymbolic aspect of the work, which makes it harder to judge the contributions and to understand the technical details. review.summary: This paper presents a neuro-symbolic framework, LILO, that learns libraries of reusable code snippets to help solve coding tasks. The framework consists of three modules: (i) a synthesizer that generates code for solving a task based on a natural language description of the task, (ii) a compression module that extracts common program fragments from a set of synthesized solutions and turns them into reusable abstractions using a program simplification algorithm, and (iii) an auto-documentation module that names and documents the abstractions so that they are more easily understandable for the synthesizer in the next iteration. Experiments show that the proposed approach outperforms existing library learning approaches (such as DreamCoder) and LLMs on 3 synthetic programming tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
- The paper is written in a way that makes it difficult to understand the key algorithmic contributions of the paper. A large part of the paper is spent describing the role of various components of the framework (e.g., their motivation and benefits), while the actual algorithm is described in just one small section (Section 3) and the algorithmic contributions are unclear. For example, the paper spends a lot of space discussing the role of LLMs and program synthesis, and the benefits of using a symbolic system like Stitch for program simplification. However, the actual algorithm of the proposed framework (Algorithm 1) consists of just 4 lines, and the role of the various components in the framework is not clear from this algorithm. The algorithm needs to be explained better so that the contributions of the paper are clear.

- The proposed framework is not compared against any LLM-based library learning approaches (such as LAPS). Furthermore, the LLM-only baseline does not use any library learning. Since the proposed approach is based on LLMs, the LLM-only baselines should be strengthened to better appreciate the contributions of the proposed approach. 

- The paper does not report the computational cost of different approaches. While it is great that the proposed approach is faster than enumerative search, it is important to know the cost of the approach relative to other baselines. Furthermore, it is unclear if the cost of calling the LLM (which is likely to be quite high) is worth the performance gains achieved by the approach. 

- The paper does not report the performance of the proposed approach on any real-world programming tasks. While the paper claims that the proposed approach is intended for building libraries of reusable functions, all experiments are performed on synthetic tasks. The paper should include some experiments on real-world code to better appreciate the benefits of the proposed approach.

The first architecture, iComFormer, is based on a SE(3) invariant graph representation while the second one, eComFormer, is based on a SO(3) equivariant graph representation. 2. The proposed method has a low complexity of $O(nk)$, where $n$ is the number of atoms and $k$ is the number of neighbors. The efficiency analysis also shows the proposed method is more efficient than the baseline methods.
3. The experiments are performed on three datasets, including JARVIS, MP, and MatBench. The results show that the proposed method can outperform the baseline methods.

## Weaknesses
1. The proposed method is incomplete. It is not guaranteed to work for crystals that have lattice containing (0,0,0). The proposed method will fail to distinguish those crystals because the proposed connectivity will be the same for those crystals.
2. The experiments are not convincing. First, the proposed method is not compared with the baseline methods in terms of efficiency. Second, the baseline methods are not state-of-the-art methods. Third, the experimental setting is different from the standard setting in MatBench. For example, the MatBench property formation energy (e_form) task has two versions: with and without standardization. The authors use the version without standardization, while the baseline methods use the version with standardization. Therefore, it is not clear which method is better. Also, the MatBench has a large-scale property prediction task with 250 properties. The authors only select two tasks from the large-scale tasks. It is not clear why the authors select those two tasks instead of others.
3. The proposed method has a high complexity of $O(nk)$ when the number of neighbors $k$ is large. The ablation study of the number of neighbors is missing. It would be good to show how the performance and efficiency change with respect to the number of neighbors.

## Questions
1. How is the number of neighbors $k$ determined? It would be good to show how the performance and efficiency change with respect to the number of neighbors.
2. What is the difference between eComFormer and iComFormer? From my understanding, the only difference is that eComFormer uses the edge vector as the edge feature and iComFormer uses the distance as the edge feature. Is this correct? If so, why eComFormer is called equivariant and iComFormer is called invariant? Also, why does iComFormer achieve better performance than eComFormer? Does the invariance/equivariance matter?
3. The proposed method is not compared with the baseline methods in terms of efficiency. Also, the baseline methods are not state-of-the-art methods. It would be good to compare the proposed method with the state-of-the-art methods, such as the methods listed in the related work section.
