review.summary: The paper proposes a sketch synthesis method based on diffusion model. The authors extend classifier guidance technique which is typically used for text-to-image generation to the task of sketch synthesis. The main challenge addressed in this paper is the selection of classifier guidance scale. To this end, the authors propose a scale adaptive classifier-guided diffusion model. The proposed model introduces a scaling indicator that optimizes classifier guidance based on recognizability and complexity. The authors also propose a three-phase sampling strategy to improve sketch diversity and quality. The proposed method is evaluated on the QuickDraw dataset.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method is a simple extension of classifier guidance technique applied to the task of sketch synthesis. The technical contribution seems marginal. The authors have adapted classifier guidance technique to sketch synthesis by introducing a scale adaptive classifier-guided diffusion model. I would expect a more significant design of classifier guidance for sketches, instead of a simple extension.

2. The scaling indicator and residual sketch seem heuristic and ad-hoc. The scaling indicator is defined as a function of stroke complexity and recognizability. It is not clear why the scaling indicator is defined in such a way. There is no rigorous justification or ablation study to support the design choice of scaling indicator. Similarly, the residual sketch is defined as the difference between two images. It is not clear why the residual sketch is designed in such a way. Please provide some justification or ablation study to support the design choice of residual sketch.

3. The authors propose three-phase sampling strategy, but there is no ablation study to justify its effectiveness. The three-phase sampling strategy is not used by the baseline methods. Hence, it is difficult to assess the effectiveness of the proposed method over the baseline methods.

They propose a scale adaptive classifier-guided diffusion model, a scaling indicator and a residual sketch for better control over the sketch synthesis process. The method also includes a three-phase sampling strategy to enhance sketch diversity and quality. The proposed method is evaluated on the QuickDraw dataset.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
- The proposed method is simple and intuitive.
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- The proposed method is evaluated against multiple baselines and ablated in several aspects.

## Weaknesses
- The authors motivate the problem with the limitation of vector-based sketch synthesis methods but the proposed method is also not generating vector-based sketches. I believe a discussion on the advantage of pixel-based sketches over vector-based sketches is needed.
- Some related works are missing, e.g. [1, 2, 3]
- The proposed method is evaluated only on the QuickDraw dataset. What about the performance on other datasets, e.g. TU-Berlin [4]? 
- How the proposed method performs when transferring to other domains, e.g. sketch to image synthesis?
- The proposed method is only compared to raster-based baselines, what about vector-based results (with rendering as images) with the same guidance?
- The CLIPScore is computed between the generated sketches and the textual description. What about the CLIPScore between the generated sketches and the ground truth sketches?
- The authors claim that the proposed method synthesizes sketches with a better balance between complexity and recognizability. However, there is no evaluation on complexity.
- Minor: The title of section 4.3 is "End-up unconditional denoising" but in the text it is mentioned as "end-up denoising".

The proposed method consists of three phases: warm-up sampling, scale adaptive classifier-guided sampling, and end-up denoising. The key idea is to define a scaling indicator and make the residual sketch (the difference between the sketch before and after classifier-guided sampling) close to the scaling indicator. The authors demonstrate that the proposed method performs better than existing sketch synthesis methods both qualitatively and quantitatively.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The proposed method is simple and reasonable.
- The proposed method can control the line width of the generated sketch well.
- The proposed method performs better than existing sketch synthesis methods both qualitatively and quantitatively.

## Weaknesses
- The proposed method is a heuristic method. In particular, the scaling indicator and the loss $L_t(s)$ are designed heuristically. The effectiveness of the proposed method may be limited to the QuickDraw dataset. It may be difficult to apply the proposed method to other sketch datasets.
- The proposed method is not explained well. The authors should explain why the scaling indicator is designed like that and why the loss $L_t(s)$ is designed like that. How can SGD obtain the optimal value of $s$ by minimizing $L_t(s)$? $s$ is a global parameter, not a local parameter.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The main theoretical results are derived based on the assumption that the Byzantine fraction $\delta$ is constant. However, in many cases, $\delta$ is a variable that is related to the batch size, e.g., $\delta = \frac{1}{B}$ in [1]. It is more interesting to investigate the effect of batch size with varying Byzantine fraction.

- Lack of technical novelty. The paper is fairly light on technical details, and the novelty seems limited. ## Summary
This paper proposes a method that learns the hidden physical properties of fluids using a 3D video. Specifically, they use a probabilistic fluid simulator that considers the stochastic nature of complex physical processes and a variational inference learning method that can transfer the posteriors of the hidden parameters from visual observations to the fluid simulator. They use the pretraining-inference-transfer optimization scheme for the model, which allows for easy transfer of visual-world fluid properties to novel scene simulation with various initial states and boundary conditions.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- The paper tackles a challenging problem. Modeling physical properties of fluids is very difficult due to their highly complex dynamics.
- The proposed method outperforms the existing baselines.

## Weaknesses
- The proposed method is quite complex. It consists of four network components, and training requires three stages. This complexity could make it difficult to train the proposed method in the real world.
- The paper only shows the results for a single sequence. It would be more convincing to show the results for multiple videos and evaluate the statistical properties of the model.
- The paper does not show any video results. It is difficult to evaluate the performance of the proposed method without video results.
- The paper does not provide any user study results. It would be great to show the proposed method is useful for the end-users.

## Questions
- How long does it take to train the proposed model?
- How long does it take to simulate a single sequence?
- How does the proposed method perform when the fluid dynamics in the test sequences are very different from the ones in the training dataset?

review.summary: The paper introduces a novel approach to infer the physical properties of a fluid from a 3D video sequence. The key idea is to learn a probabilistic physics engine that is regularized by a prior distribution learned from a dataset of fluid dynamics. A neural renderer is used to connect the particle space and the observation space, and the prior network is trained to match the latent posterior distribution inferred from the neural renderer. The prior network can then be adapted to a new scenario and used to simulate the physics of the fluid in the new scenario. The proposed method outperforms previous methods on both future prediction and generalization to unseen geometries.

weaknesses.issue:
* The method is only validated on synthetic data. It would be much more convincing if the method was able to infer the properties of real-world fluids, at least in a controlled setting such as a flowing fluid in a narrow channel.
* The generalization to unseen geometries is very limited. It only shows generalization to a cuboid that is significantly larger than the ones seen during training. What about geometries that are of a completely different shape or have a much smaller volume than the ones seen during training?
* The generalization to unseen dynamics is also limited. The paper only shows generalization to two drops of different fluid. What about more complex dynamics such as a mixture of more than two fluids, or a fluid with non-Newtonian properties such as shear thinning or thickening?

review.summary: This paper proposes a transfer learning framework for physics simulation that can infer hidden properties of fluids from a single 3D video. The method contains three stages: 1) pretraining, 2) inference and 3) transfer. The key idea is to use latent features drawn from a learnable prior distribution conditioned on the underlying particle states to capture the invisible and complex physical properties. The experiments show that the method can perform well in novel scene simulation and future prediction of the observed fluid dynamics.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The method seems a bit complicated. It has three training stages and each stage has specific losses. The Stage A and Stage C are quite similar, both of which aim to learn the latent features. Why not directly learn the latent features in the observed scenes and apply the learned features to novel scenes?
2. The paper does not explain why it is necessary to have a probabilistic particle-based fluid simulation network.
3. The method assumes that the density and viscosity are constants. This is not a general setting.
4. The experiments are not comprehensive. The method only tests on a few simple fluid geometries and the visual observations are generated by a simulator.

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a transfer learning framework for physics simulation that can infer hidden properties of fluids from a single 3D video. The method contains three stages: 1) pretraining, 2) inference and 3) transfer. The key idea is to use latent features drawn from a learnable prior distribution conditioned on the underlying particle states to capture the invisible and complex physical properties. The experiments show that the method can perform well in novel scene simulation and future prediction of the observed fluid dynamics.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
1. The paper is well written and easy to follow.
2. The paper solves an interesting problem of inferring fluid dynamics from a 3D video.
3. The proposed method shows good performance in the experiments.

## Weaknesses
1. The method seems a bit complicated. It has three training stages and each stage has specific losses. The Stage A and Stage C are quite similar, both of which aim to learn the latent features. Why not directly learn the latent features in the observed scenes and apply the learned features to novel scenes?
2. The paper does not explain why it is necessary to have a probabilistic particle-based fluid simulation network.
3. The method assumes that the density and viscosity are constants. This is not a general setting.
4. The experiments are not comprehensive. The method only tests on a few simple fluid geometries and the visual observations are generated by a simulator.

## Questions
1. How does the method perform if the fluid has more complex shapes, like non-Newtonian or complex Newtonian fluid (e.g., a mixture of two or more non-Newtonian fluids)? 
2. How does the method perform if the density and viscosity are not constants but are functions of the position and time?
3. The paper does not explain why it is necessary to have a probabilistic particle-based fluid simulation network. Since the input is a single sequence of observations, the latent features can be directly learned from the sequence of observations. Why do you need the particle-based simulation network?
4. How to handle the case if the training scenes and testing scenes have very different scales?

review.summary: This paper presents a novel modification of the variational diffusion model (VDM) by introducing a time-dependent encoder that shifts the encoded image at time $t$ instead of the original image. This time-dependent encoder, denoted as $\xi(\lambda_t)$, is parameterized as a neural network and trained during the training phase. Two parameterizations of the encoder are proposed, one that is trainable and another that is not. The paper further investigates the assumption of equal variances for the forward and backward processes, demonstrating that the VDM loss can be interpreted as a weighted loss when this assumption is relaxed. The authors also derive the optimal variance for the generative process. Experiments are conducted on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet32 datasets, showing an improvement in likelihood for the proposed method compared to the VDM baseline.

weaknesses.issue:
1. **Limited experimental results**: The experimental results are limited to the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 datasets. It would be beneficial to evaluate the proposed method on a wider range of datasets, such as ImageNet64 or ImageNet128, to assess its performance and generalizability.

2. **Marginal improvement**: The improvement in likelihood on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 is relatively small. It would be helpful to provide more details on the significance of this improvement and whether it is substantial enough to justify the added complexity of the proposed method.

3. **Limited analysis of the time-dependent encoder**: The paper could benefit from a more in-depth analysis of the learned time-dependent encoder. Visualizations or other analyses of the encoded images at different time steps would provide insights into the learned representation and its relationship to the original image.

# Review

## Summary
This paper presents a novel modification of the variational diffusion model (VDM) by introducing a time-dependent encoder that shifts the encoded image at time $t$ instead of the original image. This time-dependent encoder, denoted as $\xi(\lambda_t)$, is parameterized as a neural network and trained during the training phase. Two parameterizations of the encoder are proposed, one that is trainable and another that is not. The paper further investigates the assumption of equal variances for the forward and backward processes, demonstrating that the VDM loss can be interpreted as a weighted loss when this assumption is relaxed. The authors also derive the optimal variance for the generative process. Experiments are conducted on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet32 datasets, showing an improvement in likelihood for the proposed method compared to the VDM baseline.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The proposed method is clearly explained and its implementation is straightforward. The introduction of a time-dependent encoder in the diffusion process is a novel approach that enhances the flexibility of diffusion models without affecting the sampling process. The paper provides a theoretical analysis of the equal variance assumption and demonstrates that the VDM loss can be interpreted as a weighted loss when this assumption is relaxed. The proposed method achieves an improvement in likelihood on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 datasets, which may be of interest in the field of generative models.

## Weaknesses
1. **Limited experimental results**: The experimental results are limited to the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 datasets. It would be beneficial to evaluate the proposed method on a wider range of datasets, such as ImageNet64 or ImageNet128, to assess its performance and generalizability.

2. **Marginal improvement**: The improvement in likelihood on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 is relatively small. It would be helpful to provide more details on the significance of this improvement and whether it is substantial enough to justify the added complexity of the proposed method.

3. **Limited analysis of the time-dependent encoder**: The paper could benefit from a more in-depth analysis of the learned time-dependent encoder. Visualizations or other analyses of the encoded images at different time steps would provide insights into the learned representation and its relationship to the original image.

## Questions
1. Can you provide more details on the significance of the improvement in likelihood achieved by your method on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32? How does this improvement compare to other state-of-the-art methods in the field?

2. Can you provide more analysis and visualizations of the learned time-dependent encoder? How does the encoded image evolve at different time steps, and what insights can be drawn from these evolutions?

3. Can you provide more details on the computational complexity and training time required for your method? How does it compare to other methods in the field?

review.summary: The paper proposes a modification to the diffusion model framework by introducing a time-dependent encoder that acts on the data at each timestep of the diffusion process. This encoder is only used during training and can be removed during sampling. The authors also relax the assumption that the noise variance of the reverse process equals that of the forward process, making it a free parameter in the framework. They provide a theoretical analysis of the continuous-time limit of the modified diffusion model and derive the optimal variance for the generative process in this limit. The authors conduct experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet32 datasets, comparing the proposed method with other generative models. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms other diffusion models in terms of likelihood, as measured by bits per dimension (BPD). They also conduct ablation studies to analyze the effect of the encoder and the noise variance parameter.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The improvement in likelihood is only demonstrated on CIFAR-10, and it is not clear how the method performs on other datasets.

2. The paper does not provide a clear motivation for the specific parameterization of the encoder. The authors mention that they leave the exploration of alternative parameterizations for future work.

3. While the paper mentions the possibility of using a trainable noise schedule, it does not provide a detailed analysis of its effect on the performance of the model.

4. The paper does not provide a clear explanation of the non-trainable encoder and how it compares to the trainable encoder.

5. The paper does not provide a clear explanation of the v-prediction parameterization and how it affects the performance of the model.

review.summary: This paper introduces a new class of diffusion models that introduces a time-dependent encoder in the diffusion process. The goal is to improve the flexibility of the diffusion model while retaining the scalability. Specifically, the time-dependent encoder is used only during the training phase to parameterize the mean of the diffusion process. The paper also relaxes the assumption of having the same variance for the forward and backward processes, and shows that in the continuous limit, the optimal variance is the same. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 show that the proposed method can achieve a statistically significant improvement in likelihood on CIFAR-10.

weaknesses.issue:
1. In the abstract and introduction, the paper claims that the proposed method improves the flexibility of the diffusion models. However, it is not clear what it means by the flexibility of diffusion models. It seems that the flexibility is related to the assumption of having a constant diffusion process, but it is not clear why the proposed method can address this issue. The paper should elaborate more on this point and provide intuitions.
2. It seems that the main contribution of the paper is to introduce the time-dependent encoder in the diffusion process. However, it is not clear why the time-dependent encoder is important and how it improves the flexibility of the model. The paper should provide more analysis and insights on the importance of the time-dependent encoder.
3. In the experiments, the paper only shows that the proposed method can achieve a statistically significant improvement in likelihood on CIFAR-10. However, it is not clear how the improvement in likelihood can demonstrate the flexibility of the proposed method. The paper should provide more explanations and analysis to support the claim that the proposed method improves the flexibility of the diffusion models.

Four tool selection tasks are defined to assess LLMs' performance: tool selection with similar choices, tool selection in specific scenarios, tool selection with possible reliability issues, and multi-tool selection. Experiments with eight LLMs show that most LLMs struggle with tool selection, indicating a need for improvement in tool usage awareness and selection capabilities.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The motivation of this paper is not clear. Since existing works like ToolBench already evaluate LLMs' tool-using abilities, the main motivation of this paper should be the four subtasks. However, the paper does not introduce the motivation of these four subtasks.
2. The contribution of this paper is incremental. It can be seen as an extension of ToolBench with 4 subtasks. Also, the construction of ToolE dataset is the same as that of ToolBench.
3. The 4 subtasks are not sound. Tool selection with similar choices: The task is designed to challenge LLMs to select the correct tool from a tool list containing similar tools, thereby testing their thorough understanding of tool functionality. However, since the tool descriptions are obtained by embeddings, which cannot be understood by LLMs, how can this task evaluate LLMs' understanding of tool functionality? Tool selection in specific scenarios: This task examines how effectively LLMs utilize the tools. However, how to ensure the queries in this task can only be solved by the corresponding tools? For example, a query can be solved by multiple tools in the tool list, or it can be solved by no tools in the tool list. Tool selection with possible reliability issues: This task aims to assess whether LLMs can answer questions honestly and avoid issues like choosing non-existent tools or selecting unrelated tools. However, how to ensure the ground truth tool $t$ does not appear in the tool list $L_t$?

Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method is not practical in real applications. In real applications, the testing data may come from various domains, rather than several pre-defined domains as in the paper. For example, in the ImageNet-to-ImageNet-C experiments, the authors conduct CTTA on ImageNet-C which consists of 15 corruption types that occur sequentially during the test time. However, in real applications, the corruptions may come from various types and the model can not know which type of corruption will be occurred. In this case, the proposed method may not work well. In addition, the authors should also evaluate their method on more challenging TTA settings, e.g., ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ObjectNet.

2. The proposed method uses a pre-trained model as the initial weights. In this case, the comparison between the proposed method and other SOTA methods may be unfair. The pre-trained model may already has knowledge about the test data. The authors should also evaluate their method without using the pre-trained model.

3. Some important references are missing. For example, “Robust Mean Teacher for Continual Test-Time Adaptation” in CVPR 2023. The authors should also compare their method with this paper.

4. The writing is not clear. For example, the authors propose to use low-rank features to capture domain-shared knowledge and high-rank features to capture domain-specific knowledge. However, the authors do not explain why low-rank features are suitable to capture domain-shared knowledge. Why low-rank features can disregard the impact of dynamic distribution shifts? In addition, the authors should also show the results of only using low-rank features or high-rank features to demonstrate that they can capture domain-shared knowledge or domain-specific knowledge.

To effectively utilize ViDAs, a Homeostatic Knowledge Allotment (HKA) strategy is proposed to adaptively combine different knowledge from each ViDA. The proposed method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark datasets in both classification and segmentation CTTA tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The motivation of this paper is not clear. The authors argue that pseudo labels can be noisy and the updated model parameters are unreliable under dynamic data distributions, leading to error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting in the continual adaptation process. However, I do not see why noisy pseudo labels will lead to error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting. 
2. The authors argue that error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting are the two challenges of CTTA. However, the proposed method does not solve the error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting specifically. The proposed method seems like a universal method for TTA. Can the proposed method solve the error accumulation and catastrophic forgetting of TTA? In addition, why does the proposed method solve the two challenges of CTTA?
3. The technical contribution of this paper is limited. The proposed method is just a simple combination of low-rank and high-rank adapters. The proposed HKA is not novel. Similar adaptive strategies have been used in many works. 
4. The authors argue that the proposed ViDA can leverage high-rank and low-rank features to adapt the current domain distribution and maintain the continual domain-shared knowledge, respectively. However, there are no experiments to verify this. The authors should provide feature-level visualization to verify that the low-rank features capture domain-shared knowledge and the high-rank features capture domain-specific knowledge. 
5. I have a question about the proposed method. Why not use a weighted fusion of low-rank and high-rank features? The proposed method seems like a simple combination of low-rank and high-rank features. 
6. The proposed method seems like a universal method for TTA. Why not verify the effectiveness of the proposed method on TTA? Since CTTA is a subset of TTA, I believe that the proposed method can further improve the performance of TTA. 
7. The writing of this paper can be improved. The authors should focus on the key challenges of CTTA and explain how the proposed method solves these challenges. The authors should provide more technical details of the proposed method. 
8. The authors argue that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both classification and segmentation CTTA tasks. However, many important works [1, 2, 3] are not compared. The authors should compare the proposed method with these works.

review.summary: This paper proposes a simple yet effective method for learning video-text representations from only image-text data. Specifically, given a batch of image-text pairs, the authors propose to randomly select 3 pairs and concatenate their images and texts into one, so that the model can learn event-level temporal cues. weaknesses.issue:
1. The technical contribution is somewhat limited. The key idea of this paper is to concatenate multiple image-text pairs as one, so that the model can learn temporal cues from the consecutive text. However, this operation is too simple and naive, and it may bring some redundant information or even some noise. For example, the model may learn that the event is "eating breakfast", "eating lunch", "eating dinner", so it may think that a person must do something related to eating at any time. I think the model may learn better representations if the author use some other ways to combine the information from different image-text pairs, for example, some sophisticated ways in data augmentation.

4. The authors should report the performance of COSA on some temporal-related image-text tasks, such as "activity net" in ImageNet.

5. The authors should report the performance of COSA on some text-video tasks, such as text2video.

review.summary: The authors explore the performance of DNNs in comparison to humans in the context of peripheral vision. To this end, they perform 3 main contributions: (1) They modify the texture tiling model (TTM) to be applied at fixed eccentricities and use it to create the COCO-Periph dataset, (2) they collect human psychophysics data for object detection at different eccentricities, and (3) they test and compare the performance of DNNs on the created dataset and compare it to human performance.

weaknesses.issue:
I believe the paper is not ready for publication due to the following reasons:

1. The authors need to restructure the paper. The organization of the paper is confusing, and many details are missing. To give some examples, in Figure 3 the authors refer to a “TTM image” without explaining what it is. In Section 6, line 167, the authors say “...for each of the object present and absent images”, but they do not specify how these images are obtained. I believe they are obtained from the COCO dataset based on the next sentence, but this is not clear. In line 177, the authors refer to “...human data is reported by eccentricity”, but they do not explain what data they are referring to. How many frames were recorded? Was there a practice session to get participants accustomed to the task? Was the task presented on a white/black background or the background from the image? Was there any instruction on how to perform the task? Were there any exclusion criteria for the data? Did participants have to perform a certain amount of correct trials to be included in the data analysis? Was there any control experiment where participants just had to detect a key press? - The authors do not perform a control experiment where a non-peripheral dataset is generated in the same way as COCO-Periph but with a modified model that does not simulate peripheral vision. This would help to rule out any effects from the dataset generation process.
- There are some inconsistencies in the figures and text that make it hard to understand the results. I list them in the questions below.

## Questions
- Figure 3: What is the difference between the gray curve and the pink curve? In the text you say that the gray curve is from a pre-trained Faster RCNN, but in the figure there is no label for the gray curve.
- Figure 3: What is the difference between the gray curve and the blue curve? The blue curve is labeled “human” but in the text you say that the gray curve is humans.
- Figure 3: The legend is missing a pink curve.
- Figure 4: The blue bar is labeled “human” but it is actually human with TTM. The text is correct, but the label in the figure is not.
- Figure 4: The legend is missing a gray curve.
- Figure 4: The pink curve is labeled “Faster RCNN R50” but in the text you say that the pink curve is a DINO detector.

- Figure 6b: How do I interpret the black curve?
- Figure 6b: Why do the Faster RCNN models not have a significant effect of clutter? In the text you say that “We score the model as correct on a trial if the total object scores for the present image are greater than the absent”, but maybe this is not enough to measure the effect of clutter on object detection models.
- Section 8.1: You say that “TTM is widely-tested”, but then you go on to say that it has not been validated in color. review.summary: The authors present a new benchmark dataset COCO-Periph. The dataset extends COCO to include images rendered under a model of human visual perception called the texture tiling model (TTM). The TTM renders images by pooling together pixels in a uniform pattern from the original image. The authors use this new dataset to show that training on this dataset makes object detectors more robust to geometric corruptions, but does not improve performance relative to humans at large eccentricities.

weaknesses.issue:
* The paper doesn’t seem to have a clear goal. Is the goal to 1) evaluate how well DNNs do on the COCO-periph task, 2) have human psychophysics experiments to validate that the COCO-periph images are comparable to images from the real peripheral visual field, 3) show training on COCO-periph increases robustness to geometric corruptions, or 4) all of the above? I’m not sure how to evaluate the contributions of the paper because it has a little bit of everything. 
* The paper is missing a clear mathematical description of the TTM. How exactly is the TTM applied to the COCO images? The authors describe that they use uniform TTM but I don’t understand how that works. Is the same pooling filter applied everywhere in the image?
* How does the TTM relate to the Portilla and Simoncelli model? This is an important point that the paper is missing.
* In Figure 3, the authors compare their results to humans but the caption says the authors only used three naive subjects. The results are not convincing if only three subjects were used. There are no error bars on the human results in Figure 3.
* The authors say that the dataset is “one of the largest datasets for studying peripheral vision in DNNs”, but the dataset is only the COCO dataset with TTM transformations applied. It doesn’t seem that large.
* In Figure 5, the authors compare their trained models to the baseline Faster-RCNN model but don’t say how the baseline model was trained. The figure caption says that the baseline was finetuned on COCO-Periph but the main text says that the baseline was just the detectron2 model.
* In Figure 5, the authors say the fine-tuned model underperforms the trained model because of a decrease in baseline average precision. There is no such decrease in baseline average precision. 
* The paper would be stronger if the authors evaluated additional networks trained on COCO-periph, like the networks in Table 1.
* The authors should include a discussion of the limitations of their work.

review.summary: The paper introduces a new approach to impute missing values in tabular data using masked autoencoding framework. The idea is to randomly "re-mask" some of the observed values and learn an autoencoder to predict the re-masked values. In the inference stage, the imputation is done by predicting the missing values directly. Experiments show that the proposed method performs on par with or outperforms SOTA methods on various datasets and under different missingness settings.

weaknesses.issue:
- The proposed method assumes missingness at random (MAR) and relies on an additional mechanism to randomly mask a quarter of the data. In practice, it is not guaranteed that the additional missingness is at random and uniformly. For example, the proposed method may fail if the data has missingness not at random (MNAR) and the additional missingness also depends on the underlying data. 
- The experiment setting is a bit confusing. The paper mentioned that the missingness ratio is 0.3, but it is not clear how many samples are actually used for training. Is it the non-missing samples? Or the total number of samples?
- The paper mentioned that the proposed method can be applied to classification tasks. However, the setup is not clear. Does the imputation of missing values happen before the classification, or is it done on the fly for each batch during training? More details are needed here.
- The theoretical justification is confusing. The paper mentioned that the proposed method learns missingness-invariant representation. However, this does not necessarily mean that it is good for imputation. The good imputation should preserve the joint distribution of the data, which is not discussed in the paper.

# Review

## Summary
The paper introduces a new approach to impute missing values in tabular data using masked autoencoding framework. The idea is to randomly "re-mask" some of the observed values and learn an autoencoder to predict the re-masked values. In the inference stage, the imputation is done by predicting the missing values directly. Experiments show that the proposed method performs on par with or outperforms SOTA methods on various datasets and under different missingness settings.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The idea of using masked autoencoder to impute missing values is interesting and novel.
- The writing is clear and easy to follow.
- Experiments are comprehensive, including sensitivity analysis and ablation study.

## Weaknesses
- The proposed method assumes missingness at random (MAR) and relies on an additional mechanism to randomly mask a quarter of the data. In practice, it is not guaranteed that the additional missingness is at random and uniformly. For example, the proposed method may fail if the data has missingness not at random (MNAR) and the additional missingness also depends on the underlying data. 
- The experiment setting is a bit confusing. The paper mentioned that the missingness ratio is 0.3, but it is not clear how many samples are actually used for training. Is it the non-missing samples? Or the total number of samples?
- The paper mentioned that the proposed method can be applied to classification tasks. However, the setup is not clear. Does the imputation of missing values happen before the classification, or is it done on the fly for each batch during training? More details are needed here.
- The theoretical justification is confusing. The paper mentioned that the proposed method learns missingness-invariant representation. However, this does not necessarily mean that it is good for imputation. The good imputation should preserve the joint distribution of the data, which is not discussed in the paper.

## Questions
- Why do you choose the 25% missing ratio? How does the performance change with different missingness levels?
- The reconstruction loss is the MSE between the reconstructed and original values. Is it possible to use the reconstructed values to impute missing values, i.e., similar to the inference stage?

Besides the missing values, the method also masks out some other values as "re-masked" and tries to reconstruct them. The encoder is a transformer that takes the unmasked values and the decoder is a transformer that takes both masked and unmasked values (i.e., the re-masked values) as input. The reconstruction loss is the mean square error (MSE) between the reconstructed values and the original values on both re-masked values and unmasked values. 3. The reconstruction loss is the MSE between the reconstructed and original values on both re-masked and unmasked values. Why do you compute the loss on the unmasked values? The unmasked values are known. What is the benefit of computing the loss on the unmasked values?

review.summary: The paper considers the problem of designing neural networks that sort their input. They argue that current approaches have an error accumulation problem, and propose an error-free differentiable swap function (DSF) that is used within a neural sorting network. The DSF is defined such that it does not change the original values it is given, thus avoiding error accumulation. The network architecture is permutation equivariant, which is important for the sorting task. Experimental results on sorting MNIST and SVHN digits, as well as fragments of images from these datasets show that the proposed approach performs better or equal to state-of-the-art methods.

weaknesses.issue:
My main concern is the significance of the problem. While sorting networks are of great importance in computer science and machine learning theory, the practical importance of differentiable sorting networks is not clear. The applications that are considered in this paper are sorting images, which is not a realistic task. What is the importance of sorting images? Is it just to learn some invariants about the images? What would be some other applications?

Minor issues:
- “a sorting algorithm is a basic component to build diverse computer systems” is a bit strong claim. I would say that sorting is a fundamental operation in many computer science and machine learning algorithms, but not all of them.
- “sorting networks, which are structurally designed as an abstract device with a fixed number of wires” I don’t know what this means. What are wire?
- “multi-digit images and image fragments” I find these phrases confusing. I would just say that the inputs are multi-digit and image fragments. I don’t understand what “image” means in this context. Is it an image-classifier network? An image is not a multi-digit number.
- In the first equation of Section 2, shouldn’t it be s_1 … s_n instead of x_1 … x_n?
- “a s-shaped function” I don’t know what this means. Do you mean S-shaped?

review.summary: This paper proposes a new avatar modeling method based on NeRF. Different from existing methods, it is motivated by the observation that different poses necessitate unique frequency assignments. To achieve this, the proposed method develops a two-branch neural network that modulates the feature encoding of each point in the query space by a learned frequency. weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method introduces many modules, however, the ablation study shows they are fragile. From the ablation study, we can see that the proposed method needs both GNN and frequency modulation, and either of them is not enough. Also, the two-stage window function also needs both the spatial window function and the feature window function. This makes me feel that the proposed method is a combination of different modules, but we don't know which part is more important, and which part is less important. This makes it hard to follow. What's more, there are many hyperparameters in each module, which further makes it hard to understand and analyze the proposed method. This is also shown in the supplementary material, where each part needs many hyperparameters, and the values are different for each subject.
2. The paper claims that the proposed method can reconstruct human models with intricate and dynamic details, however, the results in the experiment section are not enough to support this. From the results, we can see that the proposed method indeed improves the results in novel pose and novel view, but the results are still blurry and contain many artifacts. weaknesses.issue:

review.summary: This paper presents a generalizable Neural Field Prior (NFP) for RGB-D scene reconstruction. The NFP is pretrained on RGB-D data from a large dataset. Given an unseen scene, it first utilizes the pretrained NFP to obtain coarse scene reconstruction results in a feed-forward manner. weaknesses.issue:

review.summary: This paper proposes a generalizable 3D reconstruction method that can construct a neural radiance field from a single-view RGB-D image. The network is trained on multiple scenes, allowing it to extract features from new scenes using only a single image. By utilizing the extracted features, it can quickly and efficiently reconstruct the geometry and texture of a new scene. Additionally, the paper introduces a continuous surface representation that improves the representation of surfaces.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method requires training on multiple scenes to extract features, which reduces its applicability. However, the paper does not provide detailed information about the training process. For instance, it is unclear how many scenes are needed for training, how many samples are required per scene, and whether the method can handle scenes with significant geometric or radiance differences.

2. The paper does not provide a clear explanation of how the geometry and texture priors are stored and applied to new scenes. It is unclear whether the priors are stored as a single scene representation or as multiple features for each scene. Additionally, it is not specified how many images are needed for new scenes, and whether a single image is sufficient for new scenes that are significantly different from the training scenes.

3. The method requires depth maps as input, making it less practical for real-world applications. The authors should consider comparing their method with RGB-based approaches and discuss the limitations of their method.

weaknesses.issue:
I have some questions about the proposed method. My main concern is the following: given that the method learns a generalizable prior, why not simply use it for novel view synthesis directly, instead of first extracting the prior, then optimizing it per-scene? This would make the method more efficient, as it would skip the per-scene optimization step.

I also think the following experiment would be interesting: given an RGBD scan, the method can be used to optimize the neural field in two stages (currently denoted "Ours"). review.summary: This paper proposes a generalizable neural scene prior, called NFP, for fast large-scale scene reconstruction of geometry and texture from single-view RGB-D images. It follows a two-stage paradigm: 1) it first trains a geometric reconstruction network to map depth images to local SDFs; 2) then it uses the pre-trained network as a geometric prior to support the training of a separate color reconstruction network, as a texture prior. Experiments show that NFP can achieve state-of-the-art quality of indoor scene reconstruction with fine geometric details and realistic texture.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The idea of utilizing RGB-D images to reconstruct indoor scenes is not new. Previous methods such as Neural-RGBD, Go-Surf, and NeuDepth have explored similar concepts. While this paper introduces some novel techniques, the overall novelty is somewhat limited. 
2. The experimental evaluation is not entirely convincing. First, the paper lacks a comparison with some recent methods like SparseNeuS and Neus4D. It would be better to include such comparisons to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. Second, the paper does not demonstrate the superiority of its results. For example, in Table 2, it is better to show the number of iterations and the training time for each method, rather than just the number of frames, which can be misleading. Third, the paper claims that its method outperforms other methods, but the quantitative results in Table 1 do not support this claim. The method performs worse than Go-Surf in terms of PSNR and SSIM, and it is not the best in terms of LPIPS. 
3. The paper lacks a thorough analysis of the proposed method. For instance, it would be beneficial to investigate the effects of the number of frames, the FPS sampling strategy, and the K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm. Additionally, the paper should provide more details about the implementation, such as the number of sampled points N, the number of nearest neighbors K, and the feature grid size.

It first samples a set of keypoints from the depth map and extracts the local geometry and texture features at the keypoints. Then, it uses the key points to interpolate the features in 3D space. After that, it trains a generalizable geometric prior and texture prior by volume rendering on the interpolated features. At last, it finetunes the priors for each scene by optimizing on RGB-D sequences. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms previous RGB-based neural fields and RGB-D-based neural fields in terms of reconstruction and novel view synthesis.

weaknesses.issue:

weaknesses.issue:
The evaluation of the proposed method is insufficient.
1. The main contribution of the paper is learning the joint distribution $p(x_1, \dots, x_N)$. However, there is no experiment demonstrating that this joint distribution is indeed learned better than models that do not take into account the context of other sources. The evaluation metrics used in the paper are not directly related to learning this joint distribution.
2. The comparison of the generation capabilities of the model to the one of the model trained only on mixtures is unfair. The model trained only on mixtures does not have any information about the individual sources, while the proposed model does. A fair comparison would be to compare to the model trained only on mixtures and with access to the individual sources during the inference (i.e., using the ground truth stems as a conditioning).
3. There is no comparison to other source separation methods. It is hard to judge the quality of the proposed method based on the Demucs baseline only.
4. The source separation experiment is performed in a weakly supervised setting, where each source is assumed to belong to a known category. In this setting, the most straightforward solution would be to train a separate model for each category and then sum the outputs. This simple baseline is not included in the comparison.

review.summary: The paper proposes a method to improve instruction-based image editing using a multimodal large language model (MLLM). It takes as input an image, an instruction, and outputs an edited image that follows the given instruction. The method first generates expressive instructions using an MLLM and then conditions a pretrained diffusion model on both the input image and the generated instructions to produce the edited image. The MLLM and the diffusion model are jointly trained. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms a baseline that does not use the MLLM.

weaknesses.issue:
- The main concern is that the technical contribution is not significant. The proposed method is a simple application of an MLLM to the instruction-based image editing task. The MLLM generates instructions, which are then used to guide the diffusion model to perform editing. The instruction generation step does not involve any vision information, and the instruction generation and editing image generation steps are independent. Thus, it is not clear what is the benefit of using an MLLM for instruction generation compared to a regular LLM.
- The paper claims that the MLLM can generate more expressive instructions. However, there is no experiment to verify this. The paper should include a human study to verify that the generated instructions are indeed more expressive.
- The paper only compares with one baseline. The paper should include more baselines, such as [1].

[1] Zhang, Xin, et al. "Hive: High-fidelity instruction-based image editing via visual prompt tuning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2307.14176 (2023).

Then, the MLLM (which is a Flan-T5-XXL model fine-tuned for summarization) generates [IMG] tokens which are transformed by an edit head into a latent representation that is fed to a Diffusion model, which edits the input image. The model is trained end-to-end, and evaluated on EVR, GIER, MA5k and MagicBrush datasets.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The paper is well written and easy to follow.
- The method is simple and elegant. I like the idea of generating [IMG] tokens by the MLLM to bridge the gap between text and image.
- The method outperforms InsPix2Pix on most metrics and datasets.
- There are a lot of qualitative results in the supplementary which look good.

## Weaknesses
- I am confused by the following statement: "To handle imprecise instructions, MGIE contains the MLLM and learns to derive explicit yet concise expressive instructions E". It is not clear to me how the MLLM derives the instructions. Looking at the supplementary material, I found that the MLLM just summarizes the input instruction. Is this correct? Please clarify in the paper that the MLLM is a summarization model (maybe even fine-tuned for summarization), and that it does not "learn to derive expressive instructions".

- I would have liked to see some diversity metrics in the results, for example on the edited images on the EVR dataset. There are many "add" instructions in this dataset, for example "add a hat/crown/flower/crown on the woman/man". Do the different models behave differently when the object to be added is the same (e.g. a crown) and the only difference is the position in the image? I suspect that InsPix2Pix would behave very similarly in such a case.

- I would have liked to see some failure cases. When does the model fail?

## Questions
- Can you provide some results on diversity as explained above?
- Can you provide some failure cases?
- Can you clarify that the MLLM is a summarization model (maybe even fine-tuned for summarization)?

# Review

## Summary
The paper introduces a universal backdoor attack that targets every class in the dataset. It proposes the concept of inter-class poison transferability, which implies that increasing the average attack success on one set of classes can also increase the attack success on another disjoint set of classes. The proposed attack leverages this concept by learning a poison for one class, which reinforces poisons for other similar classes. The triggers are correlated with features discovered from a surrogate model, enhancing the inter-class poison transferability of the universal data poisoning attack. The proposed method can be used with any trigger that can encode the binary string calculated by the method. The paper evaluates the proposed method using patch and blend triggers. The results show that the proposed method is more effective and efficient than baseline methods.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The paper introduces a novel concept of universal backdoor attacks and demonstrates their effectiveness and efficiency.
- The paper proposes a technique for creating universal poisons using inter-class poison transferability.
- The paper shows that the proposed method is robust against existing defenses.

## Weaknesses
- The paper focuses on patch and blend triggers, which are visible modifications to the image and could be detected by a data sanitation defense. 
- The paper focuses on poisoning models from scratch and does not explore the effectiveness of the proposed attacks against large pre-trained models like ViT and CLIP.

## Questions
- How effective and efficient is the proposed method when targeting specific classes instead of all classes? 
- How robust is the proposed method against defenses that are designed for targeted attacks, such as the defenses mentioned in the paper "Imperceptible Warping-based Backdoor Attack"?
- How does the proposed method perform when using triggers that are less visible or more subtle, such as natural-looking corruption, weather patterns, or other less noticeable patterns? 
- How does the proposed method perform when the victim model is a large pre-trained model like ViT or CLIP?

review.summary: The authors propose a backdoor attack in which triggers for multiple target classes can be learned simultaneously, in contrast to the traditional single-target backdoor setting. The proposed approach is based on encoding the class information into the latent space of a surrogate model using LDA and adding the corresponding triggers to the samples.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The authors only evaluate the robustness of the backdoor against defenses that were not specifically designed for the multi-target setting. In particular, it would be interesting to see how the backdoor withstands against defenses that are aimed at mitigating the influence of a single target class, e.g., by removing the influence of the target class on the decision or by removing samples from the target class.

2. The proposed approach is based on encoding class information into the latent space of a surrogate model. It would be interesting to see how well the approach works if the surrogate model is not a ResNet, but e.g. a ViT.

3. The authors only consider two simple trigger patterns (patch and blending). It would be interesting to see how well the approach works for more sophisticated triggers, e.g., [1].

[1] Li, Yige, et al. "Reconstructive Neuron Pruning for Effective Backdoor Trigger Inversion." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2023.

4. The authors only evaluate the attack on ResNet models. It would be interesting to see how well the approach works on other models, e.g., Vision Transformers.

5. The authors evaluate the clean data trade-off against fine-tuning. It would be interesting to see how the clean data trade-off looks like for other defenses as well, e.g., fine-pruning, Neural Cleanse, or Neural Attention Distillation.

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a novel backdoor attack that targets all classes of a classification model at inference time. The authors achieve this by crafting binary encoding for each class based on the features of the target class in the latent space. This binary code is then embedded into images as patch or blend triggers. The authors also study the transferability of the attack from one class to another and the robustness of the attack against existing defenses.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
2

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. This paper proposes an interesting idea of encoding the features of the latent space as binary code and using it to generate the trigger pattern. This idea is very interesting and can be used to attack multiple classes of models at inference time.
2. The authors also show that the backdoor attack can transfer from one class to another and when the number of poisoned samples in a set of classes increases, the attack on another set of classes also increases. This is a new finding and shows how the poisoned samples can be used to attack the model.
3. The authors also test their method against existing defenses and show that it is robust against them.

## Weaknesses
1. The authors only test their method on ResNet models and do not test it on other architectures like ViT and CLIP.
2. The authors also do not compare their method against existing backdoor attacks that target multiple classes like [1].

## Questions
1. How will the method perform on ViT and CLIP models?
2. How does the method compare against other existing backdoor attacks that target multiple classes like [1]?

[1] Liu, Y., Ma, X., Bailey, J., & Lu, F. (2018). Trojaning attack on neural networks.

review.summary: This paper proposes a backdoor attack that targets multiple classes at inference time with only a few poisoned samples. The authors leverage the phenomenon of inter-class poison transferability, where learning a trigger for one class makes the model more vulnerable to learning triggers for other classes. The experiments on ImageNet and its subsets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed attack.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The author should discuss the technical difference with (Li et al., 2022), which also proposes a backdoor attack that can target multiple classes. 
2. The authors only consider the transferability among classes within the same dataset. However, in real-world applications, the data for different classes come from different sources (e.g., different datasets or the web). I am curious whether the proposed method can still work in such a scenario.
3. The evaluation is only performed on the ImageNet and its subsets. It is better to conduct experiments on other real-world datasets.
4. The authors do not consider the recent defense, including neural cleanse 2.0 (NC2) (Wang et al., 2021), and DeepSight (Wu & Wang, 2022). It is better to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed attack against the recent defense.
5. The authors only evaluate the proposed method on the ResNet model. It is better to conduct experiments on other model architectures (e.g., ViT) to demonstrate the generalizability of the proposed method.

References:
1. Li, Y., Zhang, Q., Chen, P. Y., & Zhang, Y. (2022). Revisiting the Assumption of Latent Separability for Backdoor Defenses. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 15422-15432).

In particular, the proposed method leverages the phenomenon of inter-class poison transferability, where learning a trigger for one class makes the model more vulnerable to learning triggers for other classes. weaknesses.issue:

- The attacker is assumed to have access to a surrogate model, which is not a realistic assumption. It is not clear how the proposed attack can be executed without access to a surrogate model.

weaknesses.issue:

2. The attack assumes that the victim model is trained from scratch on the poisoned dataset. However, in practice, the victim model may be pre-trained on a large-scale dataset and then fine-tuned on the poisoned dataset. The proposed attack may not be as effective in this scenario.
3. The paper does not discuss the computational complexity of the proposed attack, which may be a concern for large-scale datasets.

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a universal backdoor attack against deep image classifiers trained on large-scale datasets. The proposed attack is designed to target any class at inference time, making it different from traditional backdoor attacks that target a single specific class. The authors use a phenomenon called inter-class poison transferability, where learning a trigger from one class makes the model more vulnerable to learning triggers for other classes. The effectiveness and robustness of the attack are demonstrated by controlling models with up to 6,000 classes while poisoning only 0.15% of the training dataset.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. The paper addresses a realistic and important problem of data poisoning in deep learning models, which has significant implications for the security and reliability of such models.
2. The proposed attack is novel and effective, allowing for controlling misclassifications from any source class into any target class with a slight increase in poison samples. 
3. The authors provide a thorough evaluation of the proposed attack, including its effectiveness, robustness, and scalability to large-scale datasets.

## Weaknesses
1. The proposed attack assumes that the attacker has access to a labeled dataset and can manipulate the image-label pairs contained in each sample. This assumption may not always be realistic, especially when the dataset is large and the attacker's modifications are not easily detectable.
2. The attack assumes that the victim model is trained from scratch on the poisoned dataset. However, in practice, the victim model may be pre-trained on a large-scale dataset and then fine-tuned on the poisoned dataset. The proposed attack may not be as effective in this scenario.

review.summary: This paper presents universal backdoor attacks, a data poisoning attack that targets all classes within the dataset. This is accomplished by leveraging a surrogate model (CLIP) to learn class embeddings and encoding them to create triggers for all classes. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach on a number of datasets and compares it against baselines.

weaknesses.issue:
The proposed attack relies on a surrogate model that is trained on the same dataset as the victim model. This assumption significantly weakens the threat, as it's not clear if the attack applies to other settings. The paper would benefit from evaluating the approach when there is a domain shift between the surrogate and the victim model. This is a much more realistic threat model for web-scale datasets. 

The evaluation is done using ResNet architectures, but these days vision transformers are ubiquitous. It would be great if the authors could evaluate their approach on ViT-based architectures as well. 

The paper seems to be missing an ablation study on the surrogate model's accuracy and how that affects the attack's success rate. A good surrogate model is key to the attack's success, so understanding how that affects the attack is important. 

The paper doesn't propose a new defense, but it would be interesting to see how existing defenses that were developed for single-class backdoor attacks fare against the proposed universal attack. 

The paper seems to be missing some relevant references. For example, check out the following:

review.summary: The authors propose a method for injecting a universal backdoor into an image classifier. The backdoor is universal in the sense that it can be triggered on any class. The authors achieve this by generating a trigger such that similar classes have similar representations in the feature space. This representation is obtained using a pre-trained CLIP model. The proposed method is compared to two baselines and evaluated on three different models. The results show that the proposed method is able to inject a universal backdoor in a model trained on Imagenet-1k while using only 0.16% of poisoned samples. weaknesses.issue:

For example, in [1] the authors also generate triggers in the feature space to create a transferable attack. Furthermore, the idea of generating a universal backdoor is also not novel. For example, in [2] the authors propose a method for injecting a universal backdoor in a pre-trained ViT model.
- The authors are only comparing to two baselines. In particular, I would expect to see a comparison with more recent methods for data poisoning, such as [3].
- The proposed method is only evaluated on one model. I would expect to see the evaluation on a few more architectures, such as VGG or ViT.
- The authors only consider attacks against defenses. I would expect to see a comparison with some works that propose methods for removing backdoors from models, such as [4].
- The proposed method is evaluated only on the Imagenet dataset.

review.summary: This paper introduces a new neuro-symbolic framework named Diffusion Visual Programmer (DVP) for image translation. DVP embeds a condition-flexible diffusion model within the GPT architecture, orchestrating a coherent sequence of visual programs for various pro-symbolic steps. The framework enhances in-context reasoning by deciphering intricate high-dimensional concepts in feature spaces into more accessible low-dimensional symbols, allowing for localized, context-free editing while maintaining overall coherence. Extensive experiments show that DVP achieves state-of-the-art performance.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed framework seems too heavy and cumbersome, involving many pre-trained large models like GPT-4, Mask2former, Stable Diffusion v1.5, etc. Also, the design of the pipeline is not intuitive enough. For example, why the position operation needs a dedicated model? Is it possible that the position information can be directly obtained from the cross-attention map of the diffusion model?
2. The proposed framework is not flexible enough. The current design seems that it is difficult to add new operations into the pipeline. For example, if we want to add a new operation, we need to train a new model to make it consistent with the existing models in the framework.

review.summary: This paper proposes a new image translation method that involves a sequence of vision models orchestrated by a LLM. To translate an image, the proposed method first prompts the LLM to come up with a program that consists of a series of pre-defined operations (e.g., segment, inpaint, position). The LLM can optionally also suggest a style transfer operation, which is implemented by a text2image diffusion model guided by an instance-normalized conditional embedding. The proposed method shows promising qualitative and quantitative results on several image translation tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
- The proposed method relies on a LLM to come up with a program to guide image translation. This LLM (GPT-4) is run locally on the user's machine. Since the LLM needs to see the input image to come up with the program, this limits the use of the proposed method to only local users (those with access to the input image). This is in contrast to other text2image models that can be used by anyone with an internet connection (as long as they can provide a text prompt). This distinction is not clearly stated in the paper.

There is no related work section on LLMs for image translation. In the related work section, the authors write "we recognize a number of insightful approaches, where the most relevant ones to our work are AnyDoor, Inst-Inpaint, and VISPROG". However, these methods are never discussed again in the paper. The proposed method is also not compared to these methods in the experiments. The authors should discuss and compare to these methods in the experiments.

- The proposed method is not fully automatic. The user has to provide high-level guidance on what to translate (e.g., turn the man into a dog). The LLM then comes up with a program to perform this translation. The proposed method also can not perform tasks such as "turn the dog into a golden retriever that is sitting on the chair". review.summary: This paper introduces a zeroth order optimization approach for deep neural network training. The authors suggest using coordinate wise gradient estimation over vector wise estimation to improve performance. They also propose a pruning approach that relies only on model queries and can be used to introduce sparsity for faster gradient estimation. Finally, they discuss two techniques to improve scalability, namely feature reuse and parallelization.

weaknesses.issue:
The paper has a few weaknesses, some of which I believe can be addressed by the authors. 

1. The authors mention that no prior work has shown the effectiveness of ZO optimization in training deep neural networks without a significant decrease in performance. This is not entirely true. There is a line of work on gradient compression that uses ZO to estimate the Hessians and reduce the gradient vector to a lower dimension before performing SGD on the reduced gradient. See for example: https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.04934 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.12837. There are also a few papers that use ZO to accelerate the training of deep neural networks by combining it with SGD, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.06839. The authors should compare their work to these papers and explain how their work is different and better.

2. I am not convinced about the effectiveness of ZO in the proposed framework. The authors suggest that ZO with sparsity can match the performance of SGD with GraSP. However, in Figure 1, the ZO model is only able to achieve 86% accuracy compared to 88% for the GraSP model. Furthermore, the ZO model has a much higher training time, even with the sparsity. The authors should address this issue and explain why ZO is a better option for training models in this case.

3. The authors should also compare their proposed ZO approach to other optimization approaches that do not require backprop, e.g., https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01447 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.13048. While the authors mention that the latter work relies on AD, the same can be said for their ZO approach. Overall, the authors should better motivate why ZO is a good option for training deep models.

# Review

## Summary
This paper presents a novel method, SCALE, for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection enhancement through activation scaling. The authors analyze the working principles of pruning and scaling for OOD detection and demonstrate that, within the ASH method, scaling is the key component that enhances OOD detection performance. Building on this analysis, the authors propose SCALE, which applies scaling to all activations without pruning, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD detection without compromising in-distribution (ID) accuracy. Additionally, the authors introduce Intermediate Tensor SHaping (ISH), a lightweight training-time enhancement method that improves OOD detection performance by incorporating scaling into the training process. The paper provides theoretical analyses and empirical results to support its claims, demonstrating significant improvements in OOD detection performance on both near-OOD and far-OOD datasets.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. The paper presents a novel approach to OOD detection by focusing on activation scaling, challenging the prevailing emphasis on pruning in existing methods. This fresh perspective offers valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms of OOD detection and identifies scaling as a key factor for improved performance.

2. The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of the relationship between pruning and scaling in OOD detection. By demonstrating that scaling enhances OOD detection while pruning has a detrimental effect, the authors offer a solid foundation for their proposed methods.

3. The proposed methods, SCALE and ISH, are simple yet effective, achieving state-of-the-art performance in OOD detection without compromising ID accuracy. The methods are easy to implement and have the potential for widespread adoption.

## Weaknesses
1. The analysis in the paper is primarily focused on the ASH method, and it may not be directly applicable to other OOD detection methods. This limited scope could restrict the generalizability of the findings to other approaches in the field.

2. The performance of the proposed methods may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, such as the scaling factor and percentile value p. The paper could benefit from a more detailed analysis of how these hyperparameters affect performance.

3. The paper does not provide a comprehensive comparison with a wide range of existing OOD detection methods. Including a more extensive comparison with a broader set of baseline methods would strengthen the evaluation of the proposed approach.

## Questions
1. How does the performance of SCALE and ISH compare to other recent state-of-the-art OOD detection methods not covered in the paper? It would be valuable to see a more comprehensive comparison with a broader range of baseline methods.

2. How sensitive are the proposed methods to the choice of hyperparameters, such as the scaling factor and percentile value p? A more detailed analysis of the impact of hyperparameters on performance would be helpful.

3. Can the theoretical analysis presented in the paper be extended to other OOD detection methods beyond ASH? If so, how might the findings differ, and what additional assumptions would be necessary?

review.summary: This paper explores the activation shaping method for OOD detection. It first investigates the effectiveness of ASH and finds that activation pruning harms OOD detection. Based on this observation, the authors propose SCALE and ISH to improve OOD detection in a post-hoc and training-time manner, respectively.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed SCALE is quite similar to the existing method TempScale [1]. TempScale scales the logits by a constant temperature factor, while SCALE scales the activations by a variable factor. The authors need to discuss the relation and difference between them. Besides, the proposed ISH is also related to [2], which scales the logits during the training process, and the authors should also include the discussion.
2. The proposed methods are based on the assumptions of the rectified Gaussian distribution of ID and OOD activations. The authors need to verify these assumptions on more models and datasets, especially for the OOD data, as the results in Table 1 are not consistent for different ID data. Besides, the authors use the energy-based score for both SCALE and ISH. How about other scores like MSP and MLS? 
3. The authors use a well-trained network to guide the training of ISH. How to obtain such a well-trained network? From scratch training or pre-trained on other datasets? If it is pre-trained, do the OOD data used in the experiments see during the pre-training? If these OOD data are seen, it is unfair to compare with other methods. If not, how to ensure that the network can correctly guide the training of ISH? Besides, do the OOD data used in the experiments see during the fine-tuning of ISH? 
4. The experiments are mainly conducted on ResNet50. Can the proposed methods generalize to other architectures like ViT?
5. The authors mainly use the AUROC metric in the experiments. How about other metrics like FPR@95?
6. The authors mainly focus on the semantic shift setting in this paper. How about other settings like the style shift? Besides, the authors should also include more OOD datasets like CIFAR10-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R. 

[1] Temperature scaling, ICML 2017

[2] Diagnosing and Enhancing VAE Models with a Logit Normalization Correction, ICLR 2023

# Review

## Summary
This paper presents an analysis of recent SOTA OOD method ASH and proposes two methods based on the analysis. The analysis shows that activation pruning has a detrimental effect on OOD detection while activation scaling enhances it. Based on the analysis, the authors propose a post-hoc method SCALE, which achieves SOTA OOD detection performance without compromising ID accuracy. The authors further propose a training-time method ISH for OOD detection.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
- The analysis of ASH is thorough and insightful, providing a strong foundation for the proposed methods.
- The proposed post-hoc method SCALE achieves SOTA performance without compromising ID accuracy.
- The proposed training-time method ISH is efficient and effective.

## Weaknesses
- There are some minor presentation issues. In section 3.2, the paragraph "Rectification (Pruning)" starts with a subsection "The relative reduction of activations can be expressed as", which seems to be the start of a new paragraph.
- The motivation for the proposed training-time method ISH is not very clear to me. It would be better if the authors could provide more explanation and analysis on why this method is needed and how it helps.

## Questions
- In Figure 2, why is the variance of the OOD datasets larger than that of the ID datasets? If I remember correctly, in ReAct, the OOD datasets have smaller variance than ID datasets.
- In section 3.2, how is the energy score defined? I am a bit confused because in the first paragraph of section 3.1, the energy-based score is defined as $S_{EBO}(\mathbf{x})$. Do you use a different energy score in section 3.2?
- In section 3.2, why is $r$ defined as the ratio of the sum of all activations versus the sum of un-pruned activations? Would other functions that satisfy $Q_p \leq Q$ work?
- In section 3.2, the analysis is based on the assumption that the normalized ID activations are higher than those of OOD activations. I am curious if this assumption still holds on more challenging benchmarks, such as hard OOD detection (Hard OOD Detection with Noisy Student Improvement, NeurIPS 2021) or near-distributional OOD detection (Exploring the Limits of Out-of-Distribution Detection, NeurIPS 2021). In these benchmarks, the OOD samples have very similar activation distributions with ID samples. My concern is that if this assumption does not hold, will the proposed method still work?
- In section 3.4, the ISH method is very similar to the method in the paper "Scaling and Shaping Activations for Efficient Training of Neural Networks" (ICML 2021). In that paper, the method is used for improving training efficiency while in this paper the ISH method is used for OOD detection.
